new_question:
Circumvention of the EU-Israel Association Agreement and illegal imports from settlements in the occupied territories
The ‘Importing Occupation’ investigation by the NGO Global Echo documents how approximately 20 % of Israeli agricultural exports destined for the EU actually originate from Israeli settlements in the occupied territories. Through the use of fictitious addresses and triangulations, these goods are fraudulently labelled as ‘Made in Israel’ to improperly benefit from the zero-duty regime provided by the 2000 EU-Israel Association Agreement, which categorically excludes the settlements.
This systematic circumvention not only constitutes customs fraud detrimental to the EU’s own resources but also undermines the restrictive measures adopted by the Council against extremist settlers, allowing their economic supply chains undisturbed access to the single market. It furthermore violates the right of European consumers to transparent information regarding the true origin of products.
Therefore:
1. Does the Commission intend to task the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) with launching a thorough investigation into the extent of this customs fraud to protect the Union’s finances?
2. What binding traceability mechanisms does it intend to implement to ensure that the beneficiaries of such preferential exports are not individuals or entities already targeted by EU sanctions?
3. Will it consider the precautionary suspension of preferential tariff regimes for the agri-food product categories at highest risk of circumvention (such as dates and citrus fruits) pending a comprehensive audit?
earlier_answer:
Under the EU-Israel Association Agreement, products manufactured in Israeli settlements located within the territories brought under Israeli administration since June 1967 are not eligible for preferential tariff treatment[1].
Since 1 February 2005, the exclusion of settlement goods from preferential treatment has been implemented in the EU as follows:
- In accordance with a 'Technical Arrangement' concluded by the EU and Israel, the postal code and the name of the city, village or industrial zone where production conferring originating status has taken place are to appear on all proofs of preferential origin issued or made out in Israel.
- Member States' customs authorities check whether the postal codes appearing on Israeli proofs of origin presented to them correspond to any of the postal codes appearing in the list of non-eligible locations made available to them by the Commission and refuse preference where such is the case.
An integrated Tariff of the European Union’s (TARIC) code is needed in the import declaration to confirm that the postal code appearing in the proof of origin corresponds to an eligible location. The Association Agreement provides mechanisms for Member States’ customs to check the correctness of the preferential origin declared. However, the Commission does not collect systematically information on goods entering the EU from Israeli settlements via the Customs Surveillance system[2].
[1] See Commission Notice to importers, OJ C 232 of 3 August 2012, page 5.
[2] https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/online-services/online-services-and-databases-customs/surveillance-system_en.
notes: Asks: Q1 OLAF probe of settlement-origin fraud; Q2 traceability vs EU-sanctioned beneficiaries; Q3 suspend preferences (dates, citrus). Earlier answer: settlement exclusion via postal-code/TARIC checks since 2005, origin verification; touches Q2 (origin checks); not covered: Q1, Q2 sanctions link, Q3.

new_question:
Award procedure for the Rome-Latina intermodal corridor and the promoter’s pre-emption right
In its judgment of 5 February 2026 in case C-810/24 (Urban Vision), the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that the mechanism enabling the promoter of a project financing procedure to adjust its offer to match the top offer, in order to be awarded the contract, was incompatible with Article 3(1) of Directive 2014/23/EU.
The Italian Council of State applied those principles in judgment No 3805 of 14 May 2026.
By way of public notice issued on 29 May 2025, the Italian Ministry of Infrastructure launched the concession procedure for the Rome-Latina intermodal corridor (between Tor de’ Cenci and Latina Borgo Piave). On the basis of paragraph 7, if the promoter is not awarded the contract, it may nevertheless exercise a pre-emption right and be awarded the contract, provided it complies with the same terms as the successful tenderer.
On 4 June 2026, the matter was put to the Italian Chamber of Deputies in a question for immediate reply.
In view of the above:
1. Is the Commission aware of this procedure and the conditions benefiting the promoter?
2. In light of judgment C-810/24, does it deem this procedure compatible with Article 3(1) of Directive 2014/23/EU?
3. Will it seek clarification from the Italian authorities and, if necessary, take steps to ensure full application of the judgment?
earlier_answer:
The Commission is in general not aware of the details of individual cases, such as the one referred to by the Honourable Member as it is not the best placed to investigate on individual tendering procedures. The Commission notes that national courts and review bodies referred to in the directives on remedies in public procurement[1] are primarily responsible to assess whether, according to the relevant legal and factual circumstances of each individual case, contracting authorities and contracting entities respected their obligations under EU law.
Nonetheless, the Commission takes the opportunity to recall that, as illustrated in its reply to written question [REF][2] and confirmed by the Court of Justice of the European Union in the judgment referred by the Honourable Member, the principles of non-discrimination and equal treatment, as enshrined in the EU public procurement rules, are contrary to the provision of a pre-emption right in favour of the promoter such as the one that was foreseen under Article 183(15) of Legislative Decree No 50/2016. Preliminary rulings are binding both on the referring court and on all courts in Member States and it is for the authorities of the Member State concerned to take the general or particular measures necessary to ensure that EU law is complied with within that state.
[1] Directive 89/665/EEC and Directive 92/13/EEC, as amended by Directive 2007/66/EC and Directive 2014/23/EU.
[2] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html.
notes: Asks: Q1 awareness of Rome-Latina promoter terms; Q2 compatibility with C-810/24 and Art 3(1) of Directive 2014/23/EU; Q3 seek clarification from Italy and, if necessary, take steps to ensure application of the judgment. Earlier answer: Commission is generally not aware of individual-case details; promoter pre-emption of the kind in Art 183(15) of Legislative Decree 50/2016 conflicts with equal treatment; preliminary rulings bind courts and Member States must take necessary measures; not covered: assessment of Rome-Latina or Commission plans to contact Italy or take steps in this case.

new_question:
Largest autopsy-based study on COVID-19 vaccines
On 17 November 2024, the specialist journal ‘Science, Public Health Policy and the Law’ published on its website the largest autopsy-based study on COVID-19 vaccines to date[1]. The study provides robust evidence that COVID-19 vaccines can be linked to death.
The study, entitled ‘A Systematic Review of Autopsy Findings in Deaths After COVID-19 Vaccination’, concludes that the consistency seen among cases in this review with known COVID-19 vaccine mechanisms of injury and death, coupled with autopsy confirmation by physician adjudication, suggests there is a high likelihood of a causal link between COVID-19 vaccines and death. It also states that further research would be needed to clarify these findings.
1. Are deaths occurring shortly after COVID-19 vaccination now being investigated across the EU?
2. What does the Commission intend to do as a result of these scientific findings?
3. Are people who have been vaccinated in the past and those who will be vaccinated in the future actively informed of this risk?
[1] https://publichealthpolicyjournal.com/a-systematic-review-of-autopsy-findings-in-deaths-after-covid-19-vaccination/
earlier_answer:
As the Commission pointed out in its reply to written question [REF][1], the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and national authorities evaluate data on reported events in EudraVigilance[2] to determine if there is any signal indicating causality and take action as appropriate. As referred to in the reply to question [REF][3], most suspected side effects recorded in EudraVigilance are not eventually confirmed as causally associated to the medicine administration. The same happened for the COVID-19 vaccines. As mentioned in the reply to question [REF][4], an unprecedented high number of people has been administered COVID-19 vaccines[5] and the number of reported suspected side effects for these vaccines is consequently higher in total numbers. No safety signal for increased mortality with any of the authorised COVID-19 vaccines has been identified by EMA to date.
The Commission has provided full answers to the questions of the Honourable Members related to COVID-19 vaccines, including results from the pharmacovigilance, and has ensured the largest possible transparency both as regards the negotiations it held with companies for the purchase of vaccines and the outcome of those negotiations.
In response to the European Ombudsman’s recommendation of 26 January 2022 regarding the Commission’s refusal of public access to text messages[6], the Commission confirmed the search undertaken by the President’s cabinet for relevant text messages had not yielded any results.
Finally, an action for the annulment of a decision adopted by the Commission under Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001[7] further to a request for public access to the relevant text messages has been brought before the General Court in Case T-36/23[8]. This Case is currently pending.
[1] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html
[2] https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/human-regulatory/research-development/pharmacovigilance/eudravigilance
[3] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html
[4] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html
[5] Almost 768 million vaccine doses administered in EU and EEA countries.
[6] https://www.ombudsman.europa.eu/en/doc/correspondence/en/157681
[7] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32001R1049
[8] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:62023TN0036
notes: Asks: Q1 investigation of deaths shortly after COVID-19 vaccination across the EU; Q2 action in response to the autopsy review; Q3 informing past and future vaccinees of the stated risk. Earlier answer: EMA and national authorities assess reported events in EudraVigilance for signals of causality; EMA had identified no increased-mortality signal; not covered: the study, action in response to it, or informing vaccinees of the stated risk.

new_question:
Return Detention Centre in Albania and compliance with EU legislation
On 6 May 2024, a EUR 133 million contract for the operation of the Return Detention Centre (CPR) in Gjadër, Albania[1], was awarded through a negotiated procedure without a call for tenders, following an expression of interest involving 30 entities. ActionAid reported the procedure to the National Anti-Corruption Authority (ANAC), pointing out its flaws, in particular, the failure to verify cross-border interest, which would have required an open and more transparent tender process[2].
The Commission wrote that it was monitoring the implementation of the protocol and its compatibility with Directive 2008/115/EC[3].
Once again, the problems caused by externalising migration policies need to be highlighted. In view of the above:
1. Does the contract award procedure conform with Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement?
2. What are the results of the monitoring of the implementation of the protocol?
[1] https://www1.prefettura.it/FILES/AllegatiPag/1199/Dichiarazione_efficacia_aggiudicazione_Firmato.pdf.
[2] https://trattenuti.actionaid.it/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Trattenuti-focus-01.pdf.
[3] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html.
earlier_answer:
The Protocol on migration signed between Italy and Albania in 2023 is a bilateral initiative between these two countries. Member States may apply national legislation implementing EU law, including asylum law, to situations which fall outside the scope of EU law, provided that such application does not undermine or circumvent the application of harmonised rules or obligations under EU law as a whole.
The Commission takes note of the information provided by the Honourable Members. The Commission follows the initiative carried out by Italy and Albania closely and continuously assesses its compliance with EU law and fundamental rights.
notes: Asks: Q1 Gjader EUR 133m contract vs Dir 2014/24; Q2 results of monitoring Italy-Albania protocol. Earlier answer: protocol bilateral, national law may apply outside EU scope, Commission follows closely and assesses compliance; touches Q2 (monitoring ongoing, no results); not covered: Q1 procurement.

new_question:
The need to cancel the extension of the AP-9 motorway concession in Galicia
As announced on 24 April 2024 in its package of infringement decisions, the Commission has again written to Spain regarding the infringement procedure opened in 2021 - initiated by the association En Colectivo - on the compatibility of the extension of the AP-9 motorway concession with EU public procurement rules.
In its answer to my question [REF][1], the Commission stated that it had had several exchanges and meetings with the Spanish authorities. It seems that these were unsuccessful, as illustrated by this new letter of formal notice. The Spanish Government’s decision to extend the concession for the AP-9 motorway infringes EU legislation, as the extension is equivalent to a new concession, which may be awarded only by means of a call for tenders. Spain has also failed to fulfil its obligations under EU public procurement rules, in particular Directive 93/37/EEC, as stated by the Commission.
The extension of the concession - which the Galician Nationalist Bloc has repeatedly denounced in various institutions - has the sole aim of benefiting the company Audasa. It has been a major scandal and has had a socioeconomic impact on the users of the motorway. The concession should therefore be withdrawn.
Can the Commission provide details of the latest developments in this matter and the Spanish Government’s response?
[1] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html

new_question:
Emissions
The UK Government has admitted that carbon emissions from data centres could be 100 times greater than previously thought. Revised analysis accompanying a government ‘Compute Roadmap’ shows that UK greenhouse gas emissions from artificial intelligence (AI) could reach 123 million metric tonnes of CO2 (MtCO2), the equivalent of 3.4 percent of the UK’s emissions, between 2025 and 2035. That is significantly higher than a forecast published in July 2025 of up to 0.142 MtCO2 from AI in 2035. The initial modelling was withdrawn in March in order to ‘reflect new analysis’.
In the light of the above:
1. Does the Commission wish to also update its reply to my parliamentary question [REF][1]?
2. Does the Commission expect that it will be possible for the EU to remain competitive in the AI sector while maintaining all the EU’s emissions targets?
[1] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html.
earlier_answer:
The impact of cryptocurrency mining and artificial intelligence (AI) on the EU policy objectives are on the Commission’s radar, and an ongoing Commission study aims at estimating the current and future carbon footprint of AI[1]. Taking such developments into account is relevant in view of remaining committed to the 2050 climate neutrality objective.
For 2025, the EU estimated energy use can be inferred from individual Member State reports and stands at the level of 11 TWh of energy consumption (mainly for Bitcoin), or 0,38% of the total consumption[2]. While it is not reliable to make projections up to 2050 due to technological and regulatory uncertainties, the current trends in energy efficiency gains should not be undermined, and it can be roughly estimated that energy consumption for cryptocurrencies could go down to ≈6 TWh/year (0,12% of expected total consumption[3]).
In 2024, AI data centres accounted for 1.5% of global electricity demand (around 400 TWh). Their electricity consumption is estimated to increase to 1000 TWh by 2030[4]. According to industry sources, in 2024, cryptocurrency mining sourced 50% of their electricity from renewable energy[5], and AI data centres 86%[6], thereby limiting their carbon footprint.
The Commission remains committed that digital growth is powered by clean, resilient, and sustainable energy practices. The Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) Regulation[7] introduced some transparency obligations on principal adverse impacts on the climate, for which the European Securities and Markets Authority published draft technical standards in July 2024[8].
[1] https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/tender-details/2fb0ee23-64ae-491b-9b0a-d26ff93f9a9b-CN.
[2] https://coinlaw.io/cryptocurrency-mining-energy-consumption-statistics/.
[3] https://commission.europa.eu/topics/climate-action/delivering-european-green-deal_en.
[4] https://www.iea.org/topics/artificial-intelligence.
[5] https://coinlaw.io/cryptocurrency-mining-energy-consumption-statistics/.
[6] https://op.europa.eu/s/Aa0c.
[7] Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023 on markets in crypto-assets, and amending Regulations (EU) No 1093/2010 and (EU) No 1095/2010 and Directives 2013/36/EU and (EU) 2019/1937, http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1114/oj.
[8] https://www.esma.europa.eu/press-news/esma-news/new-mica-rules-increase-transparency-retail-investors.

Earlier answer: an ongoing study estimates AI’s carbon footprint; the Commission links these developments to its 2050 climate-neutrality commitment and supports digital growth powered by sustainable energy; it also gives AI data-centre energy estimates and renewable shares; not covered: an update responding to the UK revision or an assessment of AI competitiveness against all EU emissions targets.

new_question:
Does the Commission consider children to be legally competent to make decisions about their gender?
In October 2025, I submitted a question to the European Commission concerning the LGBTIQ+ Strategy 2026-2030. In it, I asked, among other things, for a more detailed explanation of the Commission’s intention to legally recognise gender identity without age restrictions, which would allow children to change their gender at any time and at will. The Commission’s response indicates that the aim of its proposal is to protect the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, non-binary, intersex and queer (LGBTIQ+) people of all ages, from which it derives its intention to allow gender change at any age, even without parental consent. At the same time, however, the Commission refers to Article 24 of the Charter, which, among other things, states that children may freely express their views. Such views must be taken into consideration on matters which concern them in accordance with their age and maturity.
Does this mean that the Commission considers children, who have limited legal capacity until they reach the age of majority, to be capable of deciding on such a fundamental issue as gender?
earlier_answer:
Equality and non-discrimination are founding values and fundamental rights enshrined in the EU Treaties, the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (CFREU)[1] and the European Pillar of Social Rights. The new lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, non-binary, intersex and queer (LGBTIQ+) equality strategy is about ensuring that all people, including LGBTIQ+ people, are treated equally and not discriminated against in Europe. It builds on the current Strategy[2] which has been in place since 2020.
The Commission firmly believes there is no contradiction between protecting the fundamental rights of children and those of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, non-binary, intersex and queer (LGBTIQ+) people and remains fully committed to both.
The Commission fully respects the competences of Member States, and it is for them to determine the conditions under which legal gender recognition is granted.
The protection and promotion of the rights of the child is a core EU objective. Article 24 of the CFREU provides that children may express their views freely. Such views shall be taken into consideration on matters which concern them in accordance with their age and maturity.
The EU Strategy on the Rights of the Child[3] promotes a rights-based, participatory approach, ensuring that every child enjoys the same rights and be able to live free of discrimination, recrimination or intimidation of any kind. Furthermore, the Commission Recommendation on integrated child protection systems[4] calls on Member States to take appropriate measures to ensure that children are always treated without any discrimination and in a manner which protects their dignity, taking into account their personality, interests and special needs, and involving all actors, including children and families as primary carers.
[1] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/char_2012/oj/eng.
[2] https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/5100c375-87e8-40e3-85b5-1adc5f556d6d_en?filename=lgbtiq_strategy_2020-2025_en.pdf.
[3] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52021DC0142.
[4] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reco/2024/1238/oj/eng.
notes: Asks: does Commission consider children legally capable of deciding their gender (follow-up on LGBTIQ+ strategy reply). Earlier answer: equality values, no child/LGBTIQ+ rights conflict, Member States set gender recognition rules, Art 24 views by age/maturity; not covered: explicit position on children's capacity.

new_question:
Attack on the fundamental rights of environmental activists at the A69 motorway construction site
For several months, peaceful activists have been sitting in trees in the French department of Tarn to impede progress on the A69 motorway project. The information we have to hand indicates that the police response is a very serious overreaction.
Michel Forst, the UN Special Rapporteur on Environmental Defenders, has condemned actions taken by the police, such as depriving protestors of sleep by setting up floodlights at the edge of the forest, and depriving them of food and drinking water.
Mr Forst also reports that the police stopped journalists from doing their job by side-lining them far from the protests.
In light of the above:
1. Is the Commission of the opinion that France has infringed the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, particularly Articles 1, 3 and 4 on human dignity, and Article 11 on the freedom of expression and information?
2. What steps will the Commission take to ensure that France upholds the fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter?
earlier_answer:
The application of rules in respect of demonstrations, and measures taken by national authorities, including police officers, for the purpose of maintaining law and order and safeguarding internal security, inclusive of those taken on grounds of public policy, are the Member States’ sole responsibility[1].
The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union applies to Member States only when they are implementing EU law[2], which is not the case here. In the case referred to by the Honourable Members, it is for Member States, including their judicial authorities, to ensure that fundamental rights are effectively respected and protected in accordance with their national legislation and international human rights obligations.
[1] Article 72 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union states that Member States are responsible for maintaining law and order and safeguarding internal security.
[2] Article 51(1) EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.
notes: Asks: Q1 France breach of Charter Arts 1, 3, 4, 11 in A69 protest policing; Q2 steps to ensure compliance. Earlier answer: policing demonstrations is Member State matter (Art 72 TFEU), Charter applies only when implementing EU law, not here; addresses Q1/Q2 on competence grounds; A69 not named.

new_question:
Retroactive reversal of favourable administrative decisions
The rule of law is a universal principle of governance and is fundamental to international peace, security and political stability. Mindful of the developments taking place with regard to rule of law policy in the EU, the Commission published a communication in 2014 on a new EU framework to strengthen the rule of law. In 2019, further definitions were established with regard to the rule of law, and in December 2020 the EU’s co-legislators codified a legally binding definition as part of the Conditionality Regulation (Article 2).
A core element of the rule of law is the principle of legality, according to which the exercise of public powers must be foreseeable, legally certain and clearly regulated by law.
In Sweden, a discussion has taken place on the possibility of bringing in a special law that would allow for the blanket revocation of permanent residence permits. The introduction of such a law would mean that administrative decisions that were previously favourable would be retroactively amended, to the detriment of the individuals concerned. Views diverge as to whether this would be in line with EU law. With the above in mind, we should like some guidance from the Commission.
1. Does the Commission consider the retroactive, blanket revocation of permanent residence permits that have already been granted to be compatible with legal certainty and the fundamental principles of the rule of law?
2. Does the Commission take the view that the retroactive reversal of previously favourable administrative decisions, to the detriment of the individuals concerned, would be compatible with EU law, the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and the Treaty on European Union?
earlier_answer: The Commission generally does not comment on draft legislation. Accordingly, it is not in a position to provide an answer to the questions submitted by the Honourable Members.
notes: Asks: Q1 Swedish retroactive blanket revocation of permanent residence permits vs legal certainty/rule of law; Q2 vs EU law, Charter, TEU. Earlier answer: Commission does not comment on draft legislation, cannot answer; no substantive content on Q1 or Q2.

new_question:
Highly dangerous EU-supported gain-of-function research
The Commission was forced to admit that on two occasions between 2015 and 2020, the Wuhan Institute of Virology received high amounts of gain-of-function research funding from programmes under the EU framework programme for research and innovation Horizon 2020[1]. Gain-of-function research involves, among other things, modifying pathogens to make them more dangerous, more contagious and more deadly. The US administration[2], US Congress[3], the German Federal Intelligence Service[4], and renowned scientists[5] have now all confirmed that it is highly likely that the COVID-19 virus originated in this laboratory in Wuhan. As a result, the US administration has pulled funding for many gain-of-function projects that have the potential to trigger a pandemic[6]. Meanwhile, the Commission has said that it also funded a gain-of-function project in Rotterdam on the flu virus and wants to continue supporting such projects[7].
1. Which laboratories and institutes in the EU and worldwide have been receiving funding from the Commission for gain-of-function research since 2020?
2. Is gain-of-function research in the EU clearly regulated and policed by law?
3. Will the Commission follow the US administration’s lead and put a stop to or severely restrict dangerous gain-of-function research that has the potential to trigger a new pandemic?
[1] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html
[2] https://www.whitehouse.gov/lab-leak-true-origins-of-covid-19/
[3] https://oversight.house.gov/release/final-report-covid-select-concludes-2-year-investigation-issues-500-page-final-report-on-lessons-learned-and-the-path-forward/
[4] https://www.zdfheute.de/politik/corona-labor-geheimdienst-bundesregierung-100.html
[5] https://www.connexionfrance.com/news/french-nobel-prize-winner-covid-19-was-made-in-lab/375593
[6] https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/05/improving-the-safety-and-security-of-biological-research/
[7] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html
earlier_answer:
Gain-of-function research involves genetically altering an organism to enhance its biological functions and is undertaken to better understand diseases and develop therapies and vaccines. The potential risks associated with creating more infectious or deadly pathogens need to be carefully managed and weighed against the benefits for public health.
The Commission’s approach to protection from potential biological weapons is guided by the 2017 Action Plan to enhance preparedness against chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear (CBRN) security risks[1].
In this context, the Commission established the Customs Crisis Management function, enabling rapid response by customs authorities to security risks stemming from EU imports, including potential biological weapons. This mechanism has been activated in past crises such as the COVID-19 pandemic.
The support to gain-of-function research is possible under the EU research and innovation framework programme[2], subject to strict eligibility criteria and ethical conditions, verified through a scientific and ethical evaluation and screening of proposals and projects raising ethical issues, and where appropriate a security check. The programme has supported gain-of-function research on influenza virus to improve the response to emerging infectious diseases[3].
The Commission will continue to implement the highest levels of ethics integrity in the research and innovation domain, and to protect in this context EU values and security.
[1] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52017DC0610.
[2] Regulation (EU) 2021/695 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 28 April 2021 establishing Horizon Europe - the Framework Programme for Research and Innovation, laying down its rules for participation and dissemination, and repealing Regulations (EU) No 1290/2013 and (EU) No 1291/2013.
[3] Horizon 2020 COMPARE project carried out at Erasmus Medical Centre, Rotterdam in the Netherlands: Collaborative Management Platform for detection and Analyses of (Re-)emerging and foodborne outbreaks in Europe (2014-2019; https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/643476).
notes: Asks: Q1 which laboratories have received Commission funding for gain-of-function research since 2020; Q2 whether EU research is regulated and enforced by law; Q3 whether dangerous pandemic-potential research will be stopped or severely restricted. Earlier answer: funding is possible under the research framework programme subject to eligibility, ethical screening and, where appropriate, security checks; the Commission will continue ethics safeguards and cites a 2014–2019 Rotterdam influenza project; not covered: a list of recipients since 2020, a full account of legal regulation and enforcement, or a decision to halt or severely restrict the research.

new_question:
More intensive controls on amusement parks
Accidents at amusement parks and outdoor entertainment venues continue to trouble our societies, especially when minors are involved. Facilities often fail to meet the necessary safety specifications or operate without adequate control by the competent authorities. The lack of harmonised rules and inspections at EU level creates gaps in the protection of citizens.
Given that the safety of citizens - and especially children - must be a priority:
1. Does the Commission intend to propose the introduction of uniform European safety standards for amusement parks?
2. Is there any intention to create a mechanism for mandatory certification and inspections before such facilities open?

EU response to lumpy skin disease
Detected for the first time in several Member States in 2025, lumpy skin disease has become a major challenge faced by European farmers. That viral disease, which cannot be transmitted to humans, causes significant production losses, weakens farms and threatens entire sectors. The current strategy - based on the slaughter of entire infected herds - is strongly opposed by the farming community, which calls both for systematic slaughter to be abolished in favour of partial and selective culling accompanied by enhanced health monitoring, and for vaccination to become widespread across the EU.
In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following question:
Can it authorise a coordinated, EU-wide vaccination campaign that includes DIVA vaccines, as well as the possibility of partial and selective culling, so as to reduce intra-EU restrictions and limit economic losses?
earlier_answer:
1. Control measures for lumpy skin disease (LSD) are in the Animal Health Law (AHL - Regulation (EU) 2016/429[1]), Delegated Regulations (EU) 2020/687[2]and (EU) 2023/361[3], are aligned with the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) standards and based on the latest science assessed by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)[4]. Safe movement of animals and animal products require full compliance with these rules, including movement restrictions and post-vaccination recovery periods.
2. LSD is not zoonotic and is categorised as a Category A disease under the AHL requiring Union-level intervention due to the seriousness of its impact on animal health, the economy, society, and the environment, according to the criteria laid down in the AHL and supported by evidence from EFSA, EU Reference laboratories (EURL) and WOAH, and is considered appropriate and proportionate to the risk.
3. Under AHL rules, Member States have the possibility to decide whether to implement vaccination against Category A diseases regardless of the authorisation of a ‘DIVA’ (marker vaccine). Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay tests validated by EURL differentiate between field and vaccine virus strains, aiding effective surveillance and control. According to the EU framework on Veterinary Medicinal Products (Regulation (EU) 2019/6[5]), vaccines receive marketing authorisations through applications submitted by pharmaceutical companies, with provisions for accelerated assessments.

new_question:
Commission’s guarantees against attempts to weaken the EU’s environmental and climate acquis
The EPP’s recent leaders’ retreat in Zagreb saw the party adopt its political priorities for 2026. Those priorities reorientate the European Green Deal, making environmental and climate protection secondary to competitiveness objectives, industrial interests and sectoral demands. Key pieces of legislation such as the Nature Restoration Law, the Natura 2000 network, the Habitats Directive, the Nitrates Directive and the Water Framework Directive are presented as frameworks that should be simplified or applied more flexibly.
Given that those rules safeguard biodiversity and ecosystems, are crucial to ensuring safe drinking water, food security, public health and climate resilience, and form the foundation of the EU’s environmental and climate acquis:
1. Does the Commission reaffirm its commitment to not reopen or weaken the Nature Restoration Law, the Habitats Directive and the Natura 2000 network due to pressure from productive sectors and conservative groups?
2. Does the Commission guarantee that any processes evaluating the Nitrates Directive and the Water Framework Directive will ensure that their levels of environmental and health protection are maintained without ambitions being scaled back?
3. Does the Commission undertake both to not use the regulatory ‘simplification’ agenda to reduce substantive obligations with regard to environmental and climate protection, and to uphold the principle of non-regression with respect to European standards?
earlier_answer:
In line with the Competitiveness Compass, the Commission is committed to simplify Union legislation[1]. The Commission remains firmly committed to the Union’s environmental objectives and has made clear that simplification and efficient achievement of policy objectives should go hand in hand.
Article 5 of Protocol (No 2) of the Treaties requires that draft legislative acts minimise financial burdens on public authorities, citizens and economic operators commensurate with the objectives to be achieved. The Commission’s longstanding policy on Better Regulation[2] integrates these aspects and aims to achieve policy objectives as efficiently as possible. This policy predates the European Green Deal[3]. For this mandate, the Political Guidelines[4] focus on reducing administrative burdens and simplifying implementation: less red tape and reporting, more trust, better enforcement, faster permitting. The aim is to achieve the objectives of the laws with a leaner legal framework that is easier and less costly to implement.
When exercising its prerogative to initiate legislation, the Commission respects the parameters of the appropriate legal basis and supports its proposals with relevant evidence, and wide consultation as required by Protocol (No 2) taking into account the interinstitutional agreement on better-law-making from 2016[5]. It is always open to discuss amendments by the co-legislators to the Commission’s proposals in line with the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.
[1] COM(2025) 30 final of 29 January 2025, A Competitiveness Compass for the EU.
[2] https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-making-process/better-regulation_en.
[3] https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en.
[4] https://commission.europa.eu/about-european-commission/towards-new-commission-2024-2029_en.
[5] Interinstitutional Agreement between the European Parliament, the Council of the European Union and the European Commission on Better Law-Making; OJ L 123, 12.5.2016, p.1.
notes: Asks: Q1 not weaken Nature Restoration/Habitats/Natura 2000; Q2 keep Nitrates/WFD protection; Q3 simplification without cutting obligations, non-regression. Earlier answer: Competitiveness Compass simplification, commitment to environmental goals, Better Regulation; touches Q3 generally; not covered: Q1, Q2 named laws, non-regression.

new_question:
Revision of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009 and phase-out of CO₂ stunning of pigs
Each year, over 150 million pigs in the EU are stunned with CO₂ before slaughter. The method causes pain, fear, aversion and severe respiratory distress before loss of consciousness. In opinions from 2004 and 2020, the European Food Safety Authority identified CO₂ stunning as a serious animal welfare concern, concluding that the suffering is inherent and cannot be mitigated by technical improvements. The Commission has acknowledged, including in replies to Written Questions [REF][1] and [REF][2], that the PigStun project had identified feasible, already authorised alternatives in Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009[3].
No timeline has been provided for revising or phasing out CO₂ stunning. The expectation that the sector will voluntarily transition is not supported by evidence, including PigStun’s finding that slaughterhouses are unlikely to abandon established systems because of cost, reliability and competitiveness concerns. Given the suffering, the available alternatives and the Commission’s commitments under the farm to fork strategy to revise animal welfare legislation, the continued delay raises serious questions regarding compatibility with Article 13 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. The revision should include binding, time-bound rules to phase out CO₂ stunning of pigs.
Given the above:
1. When will the Commission present the revision of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009?
2. If no revision is planned, what are the reasons for this?

[2] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html.

earlier_answer:
The preparatory action PIGSTUN[1] aimed to encourage EU pig slaughterhouses using carbon dioxide (CO2) at high concentration for stunning pigs to convert to more human alternatives. Bluetongue epidemic - challenges facing sheep farmers in Portugal
Sheep farming in Portugal has been severely hit by the bluetongue virus epidemic, which, according to the National Confederation of Agricultural Cooperatives and Agricultural Credit of Portugal, ‘has wiped out thousands of sheep across the country and could spread to bovine animals’.
According to the National Confederation of Agriculture (CNA), ‘data from the system on the collection of the cadavers of animals that die on farms (SIRCA) show that the disease is out of control and containment measures are needed right away’.
There are also concerns that SIRCA could collapse.
Both bodies are calling for an immediate and free vaccination campaign and for extraordinary support to cover animal losses, as well as treatment and prevention costs, given that the costs arising from this situation are beyond the means of the vast majority of farms.
As farmers face an unanticipated decline in livestock numbers, the CNA is also warning about the risk of them being penalised by the blanket application of rules under the common agricultural policy (CAP).
In view of the above:
1. Is the Commission aware of a request from the Portuguese Government for the deployment of resources to this end?
2. Will it allow measures adapting the CAP rules to avoid penalising farmers affected by a decline in livestock numbers?
earlier_answer:
While infection with bluetongue virus (BTV) is a disease regulated by Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on transmissible animal diseases (‘Animal Health Law’)[1], Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/1882[2] categorises BTV as a category C disease. As such, it is a disease subject to optional eradication by the Member States, with the objective of gaining disease-free status. That option is subject to the decision of the competent authorities of the Member States that may vary depending on the Member State in question. BTV is therefore no longer subject to compulsory immediate eradication despite this having been the case under previous EU rules.
As it is a disease subject to optional eradication, EU funding for BTV, including vaccination, is not envisaged for 2024, nor for 2025 to 2027 BTV eradication programmes in accordance with EU rules[3], neither for emergency measures given that financial resources are allocated to the control and eradication of other major priority animal diseases such as highly pathogenic avian influenza or African swine fever, peste des petits ruminants or sheep and goat pox.

[2] http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2018/1882/oj
[3] Regulation (EU) 2021/690 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 28 April 2021 establishing a programme for the internal market, competitiveness of enterprises, including small and medium-sized enterprises, the area of plants, animals, food and feed, and European statistics (Single Market Programme) and the work programmes (adopted as Commission Implementing Decision C(2022) 3467 of 2.6.2022 for 2023-2024) and Commission Implementing Decision C(2024) 2098 of 2.8.2024 for 2025-2027).

new_question:

Recent scientific warnings have identified TFA as a planetary boundary threat due to the increasing global exposure and the potential for irreversible impacts[2]. According to recent scientific findings, the use of PFAS pesticides is a major source of TFA in the environment[3]. Currently, more than 30 PFAS pesticide substances are approved for agricultural use in the EU, contaminating our food and water resources with TFA.
