Member States should promote and respect their law enforcement rules in line with their national constitutions, and in full respect of their European and international human rights obligations. National authorities must investigate individual cases of reported police brutality and ensure that justice is served.
However, the European Union has limited competence in this area, as the maintenance of law and order is primarily a competence of the Member States. The Commission is in particular not competent to investigate individual cases of police brutality in Member States as these issues are matters for the national authorities concerned.
notes: Asks: Q1 whether the Commission will ask Spain to explain the described deaths in police action; Q2 whether it will examine police Taser use in Member States; Q3 whether it will promote EU limits or a ban on Tasers and greater monitoring of force. Earlier answer: condemns disproportionate force and discrimination, says national authorities must investigate individual cases, and states that the Commission lacks competence to investigate them; not covered: a request to Spain for explanations, a Taser-specific examination, or the proposed EU measures.

new_question:
Lack of legal remedy in the event of failure to make a referral and to comply with the obligation to state reasons pursuant to CILFIT and Remling - follow-up question to [REF] and [REF]
In its answers to questions for written answer [REF][1] and [REF][2], the Commission did not provide a clear answer to the question of whether the absence of a judicial remedy against a wrongful failure to refer is compatible with Article 19(1) of the Treaty on European Union (TEU) and Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (CFR). According to the CILFIT judgment (Case C-283/81), a court of final instance is exempt from the obligation to refer a question for a preliminary ruling under Article 267(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) only in exceptional circumstances. According to the Remling judgment (Case C-767/23), the court must provide specific and concrete reasons for the non-referral.
1. Does the Commission consider the absence of a legal remedy before a specialised court in the event of a breach of these obligations to be compatible with Article 19(1) TEU and Article 47 CFR, and if so, on what basis under EU law?
2. If not, what specific requirements does this entail for the Member States?
3. If the Commission does not systematically record infringements of the obligations to refer and to state reasons for non-referral set out in the CILFIT and Remling judgments, how can it possibly identify any structural deficits or systematic breaches as referred to in its previous replies?
[1] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_DE.html.
[2] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_DE.html.
earlier_answer:
The Article 267 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) preliminary ruling procedure is the keystone of the judicial system established by the Treaties. It sets up a dialogue between the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) and the courts of the Member States, in which the latter are closely involved in the correct application and uniform interpretation of EU law and the protection of individual rights. Where there is no judicial remedy under national law against the decisions of a national court before which a question on EU law interpretation arises, that court is in principle obliged to refer to the CJEU under Article 267(3) TFEU unless the question is irrelevant, the provision has already been interpreted, or the correct interpretation is obvious[1].
Proceedings under Article 267 TFEU rely on a clear separation of functions between the national courts and the CJEU. It is solely for the national court where the dispute arises, which must assume responsibility for the decision, to determine, in light of the case, both the need for and relevance of the questions it submits[2].
The Commission, as guardian of the Treaties, may initiate infringement proceedings under Article 258 TFEU for possible non-compliance with Article 267(3) TFEU when a Member State adopts legislation preventing proper judicial cooperation under that provision, or when evidence shows a systematic breach. The Commission monitors structural deficits in judicial cooperation under Article 267 TFEU, a prerequisite to consistent interpretation of EU law in the Member States.
[1] Judgment of 6 October 2021, C-561/19 Consorzio.
[2] ‘Ibid’.
notes: Asks: Q1 no remedy against wrongful non-referral vs Art 19(1) TEU/Art 47 CFR; Q2 Member State requirements; Q3 how deficits found without recording. Earlier answer: Art 267(3) duty and CILFIT exceptions, infringement for legislation or systematic breach, monitoring of deficits; not covered: Q1, Q2, Q3; Remling absent.

new_question:
Dutch trade measures concerning goods originating from the West Bank
The Dutch Government will introduce a national sanctions order on 22 September 2026 prohibiting the import, sale and resale of goods originating from Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
1. Does the Commission consider that a unilateral national ban on the import, sale or resale of goods from a third country or territory is compatible with the Union’s exclusive competence in the field of the common commercial policy, as laid down in Article 3(1)(e) TFEU?
2. Under Article 346(1)(b) TFEU, derogations from this exclusive competence are permitted only in exceptional circumstances, namely when necessary for the protection of essential security interests. Such measures are not to adversely affect the conditions of competition in the internal market regarding products which are not intended for specifically military purposes. Does the Commission consider that exceptional circumstances exist in this case? If so, on what grounds?
3. Does the Commission consider that Member States may independently impose trade restrictions where the Union has not adopted specific restrictive measures to that effect, and what implications does this have for the legal certainty of European companies engaged in cross-border trade?
earlier_answer:
The EU has the exclusive competence for the adoption of common commercial policy measures according to Article 3(1)(e) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) and Article 207 TFEU.
In an area of exclusive competence Member States may legislate in accordance with Article 2(1) TFEU only if so empowered by the EU or for the implementation of EU acts.
Pursuant to Article 346(1)(b) TFEU the Member States may take measures to protect their essential security interests connected with the production of or trade in arms, munitions and war material. Such measures shall not adversely affect the conditions of competition in the internal market regarding products which are not intended for specifically military purposes.
Pursuant to Article 347 TFEU, Member States shall consult each other with a view to taking together the steps needed to prevent the functioning of the internal market being affected by measures which a Member State may may be called upon to take in the event of serious internal disturbances affecting the maintenance of law and order, in the event of war, serious international tension constituting a threat of war, or in order to carry out obligations they have accepted for the purpose of maintaining peace and international security.
Moreover, Article 24(2) of the Import-Regulation[1], Article 11 of the Export Regulation[2] and Article 33 of the Textile Products Regulation[3] set out other circumstances and conditions where Member States may adopt trade measures.
[1] Regulation (EU) 2015/478 of the European Parliament and of the Council, of 11 March 2015 on common rules for imports, OJ of the European Union, L 83 of 27.3.2015, p.16, ELI: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2015/478/oj/eng.
[2] Regulation (EU) 2015/479 of the European Parliament and of the Council, of 11 March 2015, on common rules for exports (codification), OJ of the European Union, L 83 of 27.3.2015, p.34, ELI: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2015/479/oj/eng.
[3] Regulation (EU) 2015/936 of the European Parliament and of the Council, of 9 June 2015 on common rules for imports of textile products from certain third countries not covered by bilateral agreements, protocols or other arrangements, or by other specific Union import rules, OJ of the European Union L 160 of 25;2015, p. 1, ELI: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2015/936/oj/eng.
notes: Asks: Q1 whether the Dutch settlement-goods ban is compatible with exclusive EU commercial-policy competence; Q2 whether exceptional circumstances under Art 346(1)(b) exist and on what grounds; Q3 whether Member States may impose trade restrictions without EU measures and what this means for businesses’ legal certainty. Earlier answer: sets out Arts 3(1)(e), 207, 2(1), 346(1)(b) and 347 TFEU and provisions of the import, export and textile regulations; not covered: an assessment of the Dutch measure, whether the cited exceptional circumstances exist in that case, or implications for businesses’ legal certainty.

new_question:
Does the Commission consider children to be legally competent to make decisions about their gender?
In October 2025, I submitted a question to the European Commission concerning the LGBTIQ+ Strategy 2026-2030. In it, I asked, among other things, for a more detailed explanation of the Commission’s intention to legally recognise gender identity without age restrictions, which would allow children to change their gender at any time and at will. The Commission’s response indicates that the aim of its proposal is to protect the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, non-binary, intersex and queer (LGBTIQ+) people of all ages, from which it derives its intention to allow gender change at any age, even without parental consent. At the same time, however, the Commission refers to Article 24 of the Charter, which, among other things, states that children may freely express their views. Such views must be taken into consideration on matters which concern them in accordance with their age and maturity.
Does this mean that the Commission considers children, who have limited legal capacity until they reach the age of majority, to be capable of deciding on such a fundamental issue as gender?
earlier_answer:
Equality and non-discrimination are founding values and fundamental rights enshrined in the EU Treaties, the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU[1] and the European Pillar of Social Rights. The new lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, non-binary, intersex and queer (LGBTIQ+) equality strategy is about ensuring that all people, including LGBTIQ+ people, are treated equally and not discriminated against in Europe. It builds on the current Strategy[2] which has been in place since 2020.
The Commission firmly believes there is no contradiction between protecting the fundamental rights of children and those of LGBTIQ+ people and remains fully committed to both.
The Commission fully respects the competences of Member States, and it is for them to determine the conditions under which legal gender recognition is granted.
The protection and promotion of the rights of the child is a core EU objective. Article 24 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU[3] provides that the child’s best interests must be a primary consideration in all matters concerning them, where children have the right to express their views freely and those views are taken into account in accordance with their age and maturity.
The EU Strategy on the Rights of the Child[4] promotes a rights-based, participatory approach, ensuring that every child enjoys the same rights and can live free of discrimination, recrimination or intimidation of any kind. The Commission Recommendation on integrated child protection systems[5] calls on Member States to take measures so that children are treated without discrimination and in a manner which protects their dignity, considering their personality, interests, and special needs, and involving all actors, including children and families.
[1] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/char_2012/oj/eng.
[2] https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/5100c375-87e8-40e3-85b5-1adc5f556d6d_en?filename=lgbtiq_strategy_2020-2025_en.pdf.
[3] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/char_2012/oj/eng.
[4] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52021DC0142.
[5] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reco/2024/1238/oj/eng.
notes: Asks: does Commission consider children legally capable of deciding their gender (follow-up on LGBTIQ+ strategy reply). Earlier answer: equality values, no child/LGBTIQ+ rights conflict, Member States set gender recognition rules, Art 24 best interests and views by age/maturity; not covered: explicit position on capacity.

new_question:
Increasing persecution of Christians worldwide
On 17 January 2024, the non-governmental organisation Open Doors published its World Watch List 2024[1], which ranks the 50 countries where Christians face the most extreme persecution and discrimination because of their faith. According to the report, Christians worldwide are increasingly experiencing physical violence as well as pressure in various spheres of life. In particular, religiously motivated violence is intensifying in sub-Saharan Africa, while the number of attacks on Christian churches, shops and homes has grown enormously across regions compared to previous years.
1. How does the Commission intend to use the findings of the World Watch List 2024?
2. Does the Commission agree that more attention to issues linked to freedom of religion or belief is needed in the EU’s human rights policy and the EU’s bilateral relations with third countries?
3. In this context, does the Commission consider the resources and capacity allocated to the EU Special Envoy for the promotion of freedom of religion or belief outside the EU to be sufficient?
[1] https://www.opendoors.org//en-US/2024-advocacyreport/.
earlier_answer:
The Special Envoy for the promotion of freedom of religion or belief outside the EU has developed his workplan for 2023-2024 after consultation of relevant stakeholders, including religious and non-confessional organisations and civil society actors specialising in freedom of religion or belief issues, and in close coordination with the EU Special Representative for Human Rights, the European External Action Service and the relevant Commission services.
The Envoy can rely on the full support of the Commission services and the External Action Service. A coordination group with contacts drawn from the different services involved has been set up to support the work of the Envoy.
A number of country visits are currently being planned. The Envoy has already been on visit to Jerusalem, together with the Vice-President for Promoting our European Way of Life, to meet with a number of religious leaders and officials to address the situation of the holy sites and the Envoy intends to pursue this engagement.
The Envoy is ready to report back on his activities before the European Parliament or other institutions. In this respect, a meeting with Members of the Subcommittee on Human Rights took place on 19 September 2023.
notes: Asks: Q1 how the Commission will use the World Watch List 2024; Q2 whether more attention to freedom of religion or belief is needed in EU human rights policy and bilateral relations with third countries; Q3 whether the Special Envoy’s resources and capacity are sufficient. Earlier answer: describes the Envoy’s 2023–2024 workplan, Commission and EEAS support, coordination group, visits and September 2023 parliamentary meeting; not covered: use of the 2024 list, whether more attention is needed, or an assessment of resource and capacity sufficiency.

new_question:
Preventing heart disease and updating health regulations
Every year, around 300 000 sudden deaths occur in Europe - including 50 000 in Italy - mainly due to undiagnosed heart disease causing ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest.
Prevention is crucial, while survival is significantly more likely when timely interventions are made by performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation or using semi-automatic defibrillators, for example.
European sports screening models - and in particular the Italian one - have reduced the risk, but it is not enough to prevent the death of young sportspeople from heart disease.
Prevention - through thorough tests such as echocardiograms and genetic testing - is essential, but the current legislation may be obsolete and, especially in the field of sport, the distinction between those involved in competitive sport and those who are not now seems to have been lost.
Regulations need to be revised to include more comprehensive screening for all sportspeople, regardless of the competitive level, focusing on the specific cardiovascular risk for each sport. Primary prevention should start from the age of eight, with annual screening and advanced diagnostic tests.
In view of the above:
1. Can the Commission say what steps can be taken to update health regulations in the light of new knowledge?
2. How will it promote international collaboration to improve prevention of sudden cardiac death?
earlier_answer:
The Commission, Member States and stakeholders co-created the ‘Healthier Together’ - EU non-communicable diseases (NCD) initiative[1] to support the Member States in their efforts to reduce the burden of major NCDs, such as cardiovascular diseases. The initiative supports knowledge sharing, such as the exchange of best practices[2] between the Member States, and activities to improve health literacy and increase awareness among the population. The EU provides financial support under the EU4Health programme[3] for the implementation of best practices and projects that contribute to reducing preventable deaths caused by cardiovascular diseases[4].
The Member States may decide to organise specific awareness campaigns at national level with the aim of increasing knowledge on the use of defibrillators for resuscitation in the case of cardiac arrest.
[1] https://health.ec.europa.eu/non-communicable-diseases/healthier-together-eu-non-communicable-diseases-initiative_en - latest-updates
[2] https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/dyna/bp-portal/
[3] https://health.ec.europa.eu/funding/eu4health-programme-2021-2027-vision-healthier-european-union_en
[4] https://hadea.ec.europa.eu/programmes/eu4health_en
notes: Asks: Q1 steps to update health regulations in light of new knowledge, including cardiac screening in sport; Q2 how the Commission will promote international collaboration to prevent sudden cardiac death. Earlier answer: Healthier Together supports knowledge and best-practice exchange between Member States; EU4Health funds cardiovascular prevention projects, and Member States may organise defibrillator awareness campaigns; not covered: steps to update screening rules or further plans for international collaboration specifically on sudden cardiac death.

new_question:
Breach of the European Media Freedom Act by the Galician Broadcasting Corporation (CSAG)
The European Media Freedom Act (EMFA) has introduced measures to protect journalists and ensure media pluralism and independence from political interference.
Despite warnings from the CSAG’s works council and the Bloque Nacionalista Galego, the Galician government has passed a draft law affording it total control over public television and radio in Galicia, changing the way its governing bodies are elected, eliminating staff participation bodies and opening the door to languages other than Galician. Under this new legislation, the CSAG’s board of directors no longer requires a reinforced majority, and the Partido Popular government has used its absolute majority to appoint the new CSAG director-general.
Article 5(2) of the EMFA states that Member States shall ensure that the procedures for the appointment and the dismissal of the head of management or the members of the management board shall aim to ensure the independence of public service media providers.
Will the Commission check that the EMFA is being correctly implemented in the politically manipulated Galician public broadcasting corporation?
earlier_answer:
The Commission is aware of the developments the Honourable Member refers to in the question. The 2024 Rule of Law Report, Country Chapter on the rule of law situation in Spain[1], referred to the concerns expressed by some stakeholders about the use for partisan purposes of regional and local public service media.
The Commission will continue to analyse the situation of the public service broadcasters, both at national and regional levels, taking into account the Protocol No 29 on the system of public broadcasting in the Member States annexed to the founding Treaties of the EU[2]. The provisions in the European Media Freedom Act[3] aiming to ensure editorial independence of public service media providers, in accordance with their public service remit as defined at national level in line with Protocol No 29, shall apply from 8 August 2025.
[1] https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/2bd09a6f-ef56-494a-8303-e0de808ee981_en?filename=23_1_58063_coun_chap_spain_en_0.pdf
[2] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/tfeu_2012/pro_29/oj
[3] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401083
notes: Asks: will Commission check EMFA Art 5(2) at Galician broadcaster CSAG after new law and DG appointment. Earlier answer: aware of developments, 2024 Rule of Law Report noted partisan regional media concerns, will keep analysing, EMFA applies from 8 Aug 2025; not covered: new law, Art 5(2) check.

new_question:
EU state aid rules and applying them to tax exemptions for non-profit bingo games
1. Is it true that EU state aid rules prevent the Member States from granting tax exemptions for non-profit bingo games, and if so, why?
2. What does the Commission think about the proportionality of national rules on non-profit lotteries, such as bingo games, in the light of the requirements of EU law?
3. Have there been cases where the EU has previously approved tax exemptions for non-profit bingo games, and if there have, in what circumstances?
earlier_answer:
As for the question on whether a tax exemption for Federation of Aalborg Sports Associations (‘SIFA’) would be regarded as State aid under EU rules, the Commission already noted in its answer to written question [REF] that ‘[i]n this case, it may need to be examined whether televised bingo operators are in the same situation as online gambling operators in the light of the objective of the Danish gambling tax system and, if they are, whether a different treatment can be justified by the nature and general scheme (in other words the internal logic) of the tax system’.
Regarding the question on how the Commission interprets State aid rules in connection with a non-profit organisation such as SIFA, the Commission recalls that the application of the State aid rules as such does not depend exclusively on whether the entity is set up to generate profits. Based on the case-law of the Union courts, non-profit entities may be captured by State aid rules as long as they offer goods and services on a market. Where this is not the case, non-profit providers remain outside of State aid control.
In this context, it is the competence and the responsibility of the Member State concerned to assess whether a planned measure entails State aid that must be notified to the Commission pursuant to Article 108(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. In case of doubt, a Member State may of course consult the Commission on a draft measure.
So far, the Commission has not received a formal notification. Therefore, the Commission is not in a position to comment on this measure.
notes: Asks: Q1 whether EU state-aid rules prevent tax exemptions for non-profit bingo and why; Q2 the proportionality of national non-profit lottery rules under EU law; Q3 previous approvals and their circumstances. Earlier answer: in the SIFA case, comparability with online gambling and possible tax-system justification may need examination; non-profits can fall under state-aid rules when active on a market; Member States assess whether a measure entails aid requiring notification, and no formal notification of the SIFA measure had been received; not covered: a general bar on exemptions, proportionality of national lottery rules, or previous approvals.

new_question:
Safeguarding the competitiveness of the Polish and European road transport sectors
The Polish road transport sector has been at the forefront of international transport in the European Union for many years and is one of the pillars of the functioning of the common market and European supply chains. Polish hauliers carry out a significant proportion of road transport operations within the EU, ensuring the competitiveness of the European economy and the logistical safety of Member States.
However, transport companies operating in the EU, in particular in the SME sector, are under strong pressure due to the impact of the war in Ukraine, the economic slowdown in Germany, rising fuel costs, financing, wages and road tolls. The activity of Ukrainian hauliers also poses an additional challenge, since they operate outside the provisions of the mobility package and benefit from lower operating costs, such as for fuel, when entering the EU, including Poland. As of January 2026, 1 234 Polish transport companies have disappeared and hundreds more are on the brink of bankruptcy. This is why hauliers are warning that the Commission needs to act.
In connection to the above:
1. Is the Commission planning additional support programmes for EU hauliers, particularly from border countries?
2. Does the Commission intend to review the rules on the liberalisation of road transport between the EU and Ukraine, the effects of which contribute to the collapse of Polish and European hauliers?
3. Does the Commission envisage any safeguarding mechanisms to ensure a level playing field between EU and Ukrainian hauliers?
earlier_answer:
1. A study providing an analysis of the market structure and dynamics of the EU road transport sector, and the challenges faced by EU road transport operators following the adoption of the Mobility Package was finalised in May 2025 by an external consultant and will be published in 2025. It will be the basis for a Commission report to the European Parliament and Council.
2. Under the Road Transport Agreement with Ukraine[1] (RTA), Ukrainian hauliers are granted limited rights for access to the EU market compared to the rights that hauliers established in the EU Member States, as no cross-trade or cabotage operations are allowed. Modifications to the Agreement made on 20 June 2024[2] have substantially strengthened its enforcement, establishing a legal framework that enables effective controls and the prevention of abuses. In addition, as part of the pre-accession process, the Commission will prioritise the road transport regulatory convergence between Ukraine and the EU.
3. Before making any proposal as regards the continuation of the RTA, and in view of the specific concerns of two Member States bordering Ukraine and the demands of Polish road hauliers, the Commission presented a non-paper with options to Member States on 14 July 2025. This non-paper was discussed at the Council Land Transport Working Parties of 17 and 22 July 2025.
[1] Agreement between the European Union and Ukraine on the carriage of freight by road (OJ L 179, 6.7.2022, p. 4).
[2] Agreement between the European Union and Ukraine amending the Agreement between the European Union and Ukraine on the Carriage of Freight by Road of 29 June 2022 (OJ L 2024/1878, 2.7.2024).
notes: Asks: Q1 support for hauliers in border states; Q2 review EU-Ukraine road liberalisation; Q3 level-playing-field safeguards. Earlier answer: Mobility Package study (2025); RTA bars cabotage/cross-trade, June 2024 enforcement changes; July 2025 options non-paper; touches Q2, Q3; not covered: Q1.

new_question:
Accountability of Airbus in the Privatisation of TAP
The Inspectorate-General of Finance of the Portuguese Republic has carried out an audit that points to the participation of Airbus - a European multinational - in an illegal and criminal scheme for financing TAP’s privatisation in 2015.
The same conclusion had already been reached by a Portuguese Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry, whose work was completed a year ago. At that time, the Assembly of the Republic asked the Government to request that the European Union investigate that participation and establish the necessary accountabilities for the difficulties that said participation created for the Portuguese Republic.
In the meantime, the Portuguese Prime Minister has informed the Assembly of the Republic that the Government has not taken ‘any steps’ to implement that resolution of the Assembly of the Republic. This was a regrettable choice, but one that only serves to hold accountable those to made it (the last two Portuguese governments).
But the question was already referred directly to the European Commission (questions [REF][1] and [REF][2]), so we are asking again:
1. Has the European Commission already carried out an assessment of the role played by Airbus in the privatisation process of TAP, in 2015, and its accountability for the damage caused to the Portuguese Republic by that privatisation?
2. If so, what are the results of that assessment? If not, why has no assessment been carried out?
[1] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html
[2] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html
earlier_answer:
It is understood that by the first question, the Honourable Member is referring to a request the Portuguese Parliament made to the Portuguese Government to contact the EU institutions in relation to the alleged implication of Airbus in TAP privatisation process. The Commission is not in a position to intervene in the relations between national governing institutions of a Member State or to comment on ongoing investigations of national courts of the Member States.
When invited, the Commission always cooperates with national parliaments and provides answers in writing to the questions that parliaments submit to the Commission. In line with that practice, the Commission has replied to three requests for information of the Portuguese Parliament’s Committee of Inquiry, received on 13 March and on 7 June 2023, by letters of 24 May, 28 July and 1 August 2023. The Commission confirms that it has processed the replies to those requests as quickly as possible, in line with its standard procedures, also considering the sensitivity and complexity of the issues raised by the Parliamentary Committee.
Finally, the circumstances referred to in the Honourable Member’s question [REF] took place several years before the notification of rescue and restructuring aid to TAP and were not part of the Commission’s assessment in its decisions approving these aid measures[1].
[1]See Commission Decision C(2021) 5302 final of 16 July 2021 in case SA.57369 (2020/N) - Portugal - Rescue aid to TAP SGPS (OJ C 345, 27.8.2021, p. 1) adopted following the annulment of Commission Decision C(2020) 3989 final of 10 June 2020 in case SA.57369 (2020/N) - COVID 19 - Portugal - Aid to TAP (OJ C 228, 10.7.2020, p. 1) and Commission Decision C(2021) 9941 final of 21 December 2021 in case SA.60165 (2021/C (ex 2021/N) on the State aid which Portugal is planning to implement for TAP SGPS (OJ L 139, 18.5.2022, p. 19).
notes: Asks: Q1 has Commission assessed Airbus role in 2015 TAP privatisation; Q2 results or why not. Earlier answer: cannot intervene in national relations or comment on national probes; answered PT inquiry in 2023; 2015 events outside TAP state aid assessments; touches Q1/Q2 (not in aid decisions); no Airbus assessment described.

new_question:
Tender procedure for the granting of a concession for a waste-to-energy plant in the Municipality of Rome
With its public notice of 16 November 2023, the Municipality of Rome Capital launched a tender procedure for the granting of a concession to build a waste-to-energy plant with a capacity of approximately 600 000 tonnes of waste per year.
The procedure was carried out through project financing under Article 183(15) of Legislative Decree No 50/2016, which provides for the possibility of the promoter exercising a pre-emption right.
In its judgment of 5 February 2026 (Case C-810/24), the Court of Justice ruled that Article 3(1) of Directive 2014/23/EU, read in conjunction with EU law and other provisions of that directive, precludes a Member State from granting the promoter of a project financing procedure a right of pre-emption.
In light of the above:
1. Can the Commission confirm how many economic operators submitted requests for participation, and was the concession awarded to the promoter?
2. Is it possible that the provision of a pre-emption right discouraged other economic operators from participating?
3. Did the tender procedure have distortive effects on competition, in breach of the principles of non-discrimination and equal treatment under EU law?
earlier_answer:
The Commission recalls that according to the principle of free administration by public authorities enshrined in Article 2 of Directive 2014/23/EU[1], Member States authorities may choose to perform their public interest tasks with their own resources, or in cooperation with other authorities or to confer them upon economic operators.
As illustrated in the answer given to written question [REF], a concession within the meaning of Directive 2014/23/EU, such as the A22 motorway concession referred to by the Honourable Members, may be awarded without a call for tenders if the in-house requirements under Article 17 of that Directive are fulfilled. However, if the in-house requirements, including the absence of private capital in the concessionaire company, were not all fulfilled, the concession would have to be awarded via a call for tenders ensuring fair competition under the rules set out in that Directive.
According to the principles of non-discrimination and equal treatment as enshrined in the EU public procurement rules, it is of utmost importance that any eventual participation of the incumbent concessionaire in the tendering procedure should be accompanied by the adoption of the appropriate mitigation measures to ensure that competition is not distorted.[2] In the case at hand, the project financing award procedure providing for a pre-emption right for the incumbent concessionaire raises serious concerns with regard to its compatibility with EU law. The Commission is in touch with the Italian authorities and closely monitors the file.
[1] Directive 2014/23/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 February 2014 on the award of concession contracts (OJ L 094 28.3.2014, p. 1).
[2] Ibid., articles 3, 35; Directive 2014/24/EU, articles 18, 41.
notes: Asks: Q1 number of participation requests and whether the Rome plant concession went to the promoter; Q2 whether pre-emption discouraged other operators; Q3 whether the procedure distorted competition and breached equal treatment and non-discrimination. Earlier answer: discusses the A22 concession, in-house requirements and measures to prevent distortion; says the incumbent's pre-emption right raises serious EU-law concerns and the Commission is in contact with Italy; not covered: the Rome procedure, its participation figures and award, or whether pre-emption deterred its bidders.

new_question:
Natural disasters caused by climate change
Recently a number of countries have been hit by natural disasters with extreme weather conditions causing deadly forest fires and flooding, leading to many areas being evacuated and leaving thousands of people displaced. Greece was especially hard-hit by wildfires, notably in Rhodes, Attica, Evros and Thessaly. In light of these disasters, our thoughts are constantly with the inhabitants of the affected areas, with the women and men working for the fire service, the security forces and the volunteers who fought to keep people safe.
In view of this:
1. Will the Commission take any additional prevention measures to protect nature and human safety and address the effects of climate change, thereby supporting areas that have taken a hit economically?
2. Will it review the Civil Protection Mechanism, which should be adapted to address the ever-growing consequences of climate change and monitor the funding that will be given to affected countries?
3. Will it increase funding in the budget to support Member States and review the Solidarity Fund so that more help is given to countries affected by natural disasters caused by climate change?
earlier_answer:
1. The EU supports prevention projects for damage caused by natural disasters through several channels. The Multiannual Financial Framework 2021-27[1] ensures that at least 25% of the European budget is climate-related expenditure, which includes climate adaptation specific actions. The European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) provides funding for civil protection, environment, and climate. Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) plans[2] allocate at least 37% (37.5% for Greece) of their expenditure to climate objectives. The Greek plan includes more than EUR 600 million investments in reforestation, biodiversity, flood mitigation and irrigation network upgrades. Horizon Europe[3] funds disaster (including climate related) risk reduction research. The EU Civil Protection Mechanism[4] launches a call for financing prevention and preparedness projects annually. The EU Solidarity Fund (EUSF)[5] supports Member States in disaster relief and public infrastructure restoration among others.
2. The ERDF Programme for Central Macedonia for 2014-20 invested in the prevention of floods and other related damage caused by climate change, including nine projects in the Thessaloniki metropolitan area. By 2022 payments amounted to EUR 21.4 million. The Programme for Central Macedonia for 2021-27, supported through ERDF and the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+), has earmarked EUR 34.7 million for flood and landslide protection projects in the region. The Programme for Environment and Climate Change 2021-27 allocates EUR 132 million to antiflood projects across Greece.
The EUSF has assisted Greece in 13 instances following natural disasters, but it has not supported the Central Macedonia region nor Thessaloniki so far.
[1] https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/eu-budget/long-term-eu-budget/2021-2027_en
[2] https://commission.europa.eu/business-economy-euro/economic-recovery/recovery-and-resilience-facility_en
[3] https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-open-calls/horizon-europe_en
[4] https://civil-protection-humanitarian-aid.ec.europa.eu/funding-evaluations/financing-civil-protection/prevention-and-preparedness-projects-civil-protection_en
[5] https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/funding/solidarity-fund_en, Council Regulation (EC) No 2012/2002 of 11 November 2002 establishing the EU Solidarity Fund (OJ L 311, 14.11.2002, p. 3) as amended by Regulation (EU) No 661/2014 of the European Parliament and the Council of 15 May 2014 (OJ L 189, 27.6.2014, p. 143) and by Regulation (EU) 2020/461 of the European Parliament and the Council of 30 March 2020 (OJ L 99, 31.3.2020, p. 9). The EUSF can only be activated at the request of the affected state. within 12 weeks of the first damage occurred, demonstrating that the total direct damage exceeds the thresholds specified in Article 2 Regulation (EC) No 2012/2002. The EUSF may cover a part of the costs for emergency and recovery operations incurred by public authorities. The Commission thus clearly stated that it considers these allegations to be untrue and strongly distances itself from them.
1. I assume that, since the publication of the US report up to the present day, the Commission has already taken specific diplomatic, political and legal steps to actively safeguard the integrity of its actions and public trust; if not, why not?
2. Has the Commission formally approached-by diplomatic note, official letter or other official means-the United States House Judiciary Committee, its Chair, or the US Congress with a request for a public correction, retraction, or withdrawal of the false allegations concerning interference in the Slovak elections?
3. Beyond the brief response to my written question, what other public steps (press releases, statements, media briefings or other forms of communication) has the Commission taken vis-à-vis the European public to actively refute these allegations and defend its credibility?

earlier_answer:
The Commission firmly rejects the report’s unfounded and unsubstantiated allegations, including those concerning Slovakia’s 2023 elections.
Freedom of expression is a cornerstone of the Digital Services Act (DSA)[1]. It helps protect this freedom by entitling users to explanations, appeals and redress when their content is removed or restricted by platforms.
The DSA does not prescribe which content is illegal; this is determined purely by national law or other EU laws. The Commission does not have the competence to mandate the removal of specific items of lawful content; moderation decisions lie with platforms themselves. Since its application, 30% of appealed moderation decisions[2] have been reversed, proving users have real recourse mechanisms. No other law matches the DSA’s protections against arbitrary platform moderation or its demand for accountability on how platforms operate.
TikTok’s alleged content removals must therefore stem from its own policies. The DSA ensures accountability and transparency through annual transparency reports, where platforms must justify restriction or removal of content (e.g., under legal provisions or terms of service). Compliance is annually checked by an external audit.
The DSA also requires very large online platforms to assess systemic risks to civic discourse and elections, while considering the exercise of fundamental rights, including the right to freedom of expression and information[3]. Engaging with platforms to ask how their systems and practices operate across different jurisdictions is a normal and necessary part of regulatory oversight. Interpreting such exchanges as a wish to influence political debate or pressure platforms misrepresents the nature of regulatory dialogue.
[1] Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 on a single market for digital services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act), https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng.
[2] https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/two-years-digital-services-act-allows-50-million-content-moderation-decisions-platforms-be-reversed.
[3] Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/char_2012/oj/eng.
notes: Asks: Q1 diplomatic, political and legal steps since the US House report to safeguard integrity and public trust, or why none were taken; Q2 whether the Commission formally requested a correction, retraction or withdrawal from US officials; Q3 other public steps to refute the allegations. Earlier answer: rejects the report's allegations, including those concerning Slovakia's 2023 elections, and describes DSA safeguards, TikTok moderation and regulatory dialogue; not covered: the requested steps or explanation beyond the cited reply.

new_question:
Lack of awareness regarding the European Health Insurance Card
The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) is an important tool that provides EU citizens with access to necessary medical care during a temporary stay in another Member State under the same conditions as the residents of that country. Although the EHIC is available free of charge and is based on directly applicable EU regulations, in practice many insured persons are insufficiently aware of the existence, purpose and scope of this card. This lack of awareness can lead to unnecessary costs, administrative problems and barriers to accessing healthcare. It also raises questions about the effectiveness of the current provision of information by health and travel insurers within Member States.
1. What is the Commission’s assessment of the current provision of information by health insurers regarding the availability of the EHIC?
2. What can the Commission do to ensure that health insurers publicise the EHIC more widely?
earlier_answer:
The Commission’s Work Programme for 2026 announces a Fair Labour Mobility Package which includes an initiative for the European Social Security Pass (ESSPASS)[1]. A digitalised European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) is one of the objectives of the ESSPASS initiative.

A second piloted approach considers a QR-code based format, targeting citizens who may have difficulties using a digital wallet.

new_question:
Opening up a way for social enterprises
According to the judgment of the Court of Justice of 8 September 2011 in Joined Cases C-78/08 to 80/08, third-sector bodies can be considered as belonging to a category of organisations that guarantee ‘social freedoms’, thereby entitling them to certain benefits. The indifference being shown by the Commission is of great concern, as it is effectively preventing the actual implementation of new social enterprises and has left this sector, which is clearly growing, in a state of limbo when it comes to planning. In view of this:
1. Why is the Commission refusing to comment on the measures set out in Italy’s Third Sector Code and why is it insisting on having the Italian Government notify it of something that has already been explicitly regulated - namely that non-profit organisations covered by the Third Sector Code and listed in the National Single Register of the Third Sector (RUNTS) are entitled to State aid as economic enterprises offering goods and services and falling under the exemptions for protected categories?
2. Can the Commission explain what measures involving State aid it is that have not already been notified under the Third Sector Code and should be notified by the Italian Government to the Commission for its opinion?
earlier_answer:
The Commission understands that the Italian Code for the third sector makes the entry into force of some of its material rules concerning some of the entities featuring in the RUNTS Register conditional upon those rules being first notified to the Commission, under Article 108(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU.
Under EU State aid rules, it is the responsibility of Member States to notify or inform the Commission about measures that entail State aid, unless they are covered by block exemptions. As of today, no such notification has been made. Therefore, the Commission is not in a position to comment on this measure. In order to constitute State aid, a measure must fulfil all the conditions laid down in Article 107(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.
notes: Asks: Q1 why Commission won't comment on Italian Third Sector Code and requires notification; Q2 which State-aid measures still need notifying. new_question:
EU-prescribed diesel engine additive does not work in freezing conditions
Finland has recently experienced severe frosts throughout the country. The lowest temperature recorded so far this year has been -42.8°C, in Lapland. It has become apparent that EU legislation does not take enough account of the different weather conditions in the Member States. Furthermore, sufficient requirements are not in place obliging vehicle manufacturers to take into account the reliability of emission reduction systems in cold conditions such as those commonly experienced in Finland.
Current emission reduction equipment for diesel cars cannot withstand Finnish winter temperatures, and up to 80 % of transport companies have experienced problems owing to the AdBlue urea solution freezing. In practice, AdBlue fluid is required by the EU to reduce nitrogen oxide emissions, but it freezes at around -11°C.
The problem is widespread, as the freezing of the AdBlue urea solution increases the risk of equipment failure, affecting not only cars but machinery as well, and resulting in significant additional costs for sectors such as transport, forestry, agriculture, mining, public transport and tourism. The vulnerability of the systems to normal freezing conditions is also having a negative impact on Finland’s security of supply.
1. Is the Commission aware that the AdBlue urea solution, which is effectively required under by EU regulations, does not work in normal winter conditions in Finland, causing unnecessary additional costs and having an adverse impact on Finland’s security of supply?
2. Will the Commission permit, as a matter of urgency, alternative, more frost-resistant additives to reduce nitrogen oxide emissions from diesel cars?
3. Does the Commission intend to take better account of northern conditions, and of the specific characteristics of the north, in EU regulation in the future?
earlier_answer:
The Commission is aware of the problem of using reagents in extremely cold temperatures. The Commission has been informed about the results of a survey conducted by the Finnish Transport and Logistics Association SKAL on this topic.
The Commission sees various possible solutions to alleviate these difficulties, such as the industry-led development of a new standard for increased frost resistance to improve the performance of reagents in extremely cold conditions or the use of reagents with a lower freezing point. The specific requirements for reagents, especially the physical properties, are not regulated by EU law, which would allow the use of alternative reagents with a lower freezing point in colder weather conditions, provided that manufacturers would admit such a reagent for the use.
notes: Asks: Q1 whether the Commission is aware of AdBlue problems in Finnish winter conditions, their costs and effects on security of supply; Q2 whether it will allow more frost-resistant additives; Q3 whether future EU rules will better account for northern conditions. Earlier answer: is aware of cold-temperature reagent problems and a SKAL survey; identifies a possible frost-resistance standard and says EU law permits lower-freezing-point reagents if manufacturers admit them; not covered: the claimed costs and security-of-supply effects, or future rules accounting for northern conditions.

new_question:
Breach of the European Media Freedom Act by the Galician Broadcasting Corporation (CSAG)
The European Media Freedom Act (EMFA) has introduced measures to protect journalists and ensure media pluralism and independence from political interference.
Despite warnings from the CSAG’s works council and the Bloque Nacionalista Galego, the Galician government has passed a draft law affording it total control over public television and radio in Galicia, changing the way its governing bodies are elected, eliminating staff participation bodies and opening the door to languages other than Galician. Under this new legislation, the CSAG’s board of directors no longer requires a reinforced majority, and the Partido Popular government has used its absolute majority to appoint the new CSAG director-general.
Article 5(2) of the EMFA states that Member States shall ensure that the procedures for the appointment and the dismissal of the head of management or the members of the management board shall aim to ensure the independence of public service media providers.
Will the Commission check that the EMFA is being correctly implemented in the politically manipulated Galician public broadcasting corporation?
earlier_answer:
The Commission is aware of the developments the Honourable Member refers to in the question. The EU upholds linguistic diversity and the promotion of regional and minority languages. However, Member States are responsible for their cultural and linguistic diversity[1]. It follows that the legal provisions governing the use of languages fall within the exclusive competence of the Member States and must therefore be addressed at national level. Also, the Commission does not monitor the implementation of the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages[2] of the Council of Europe.
The provisions of the European Media Freedom Act[3] aiming to ensure editorial independence of public service media providers and provision by them of a plurality of information and opinions to their audiences, in accordance with their public service remit as defined at national level, in line with Protocol No 29 on the system of public broadcasting in the Member States annexed to the founding Treaties of the EU[4], shall apply from 8 August 2025.
More generally, the Commission will continue to monitor developments regarding the situation of the public service broadcasters, taking into account Protocol No 29, in particular in its annual Rule of Law report[5].
[1] Article 165 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.
[2] https://www.coe.int/en/web/european-charter-regional-or-minority-languages/text-of-the-charter
[3] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401083
[4] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/tfeu_2012/pro_29/oj
[5] https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/2bd09a6f-ef56-494a-8303-e0de808ee981_en
notes: Asks: whether the Commission will check EMFA compliance in the Galician public broadcaster, including its governance and director appointment. Earlier answer: is aware of developments; says language rules are a national competence, EMFA public-service media provisions apply from 8 August 2025, and it will monitor public broadcasters, including in the Rule of Law report; not covered: an assessment of the CSAG appointment or governance under the EMFA.

new_question:
Does the Commission consider children to be legally competent to make decisions about their gender?
In October 2025, I submitted a question to the European Commission concerning the LGBTIQ+ Strategy 2026-2030. In it, I asked, among other things, for a more detailed explanation of the Commission’s intention to legally recognise gender identity without age restrictions, which would allow children to change their gender at any time and at will. The Commission’s response indicates that the aim of its proposal is to protect the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, non-binary, intersex and queer (LGBTIQ+) people of all ages, from which it derives its intention to allow gender change at any age, even without parental consent. At the same time, however, the Commission refers to Article 24 of the Charter, which, among other things, states that children may freely express their views. Such views must be taken into consideration on matters which concern them in accordance with their age and maturity.
Does this mean that the Commission considers children, who have limited legal capacity until they reach the age of majority, to be capable of deciding on such a fundamental issue as gender?
earlier_answer:
The Commission adopted a new LGBTIQ+[1] equality strategy 2026-2030[2] on 8 October 2025.
The Commission firmly believes that the protection of children and the safeguarding of the fundamental rights of the LGBTIQ+ community are not mutually exclusive, remaining strongly and equally committed to both.
Equality and non-discrimination are founding values and fundamental rights enshrined in the EU Treaties, the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union[3] and the European Pillar of Social Rights. The new LGBTIQ+ equality strategy is precisely about ensuring that all people, including LGBTIQ+ people, are treated equally and not discriminated against in Europe. It builds on the current Strategy[4] which has been in place since 2020.
The Commission fully respects the competences of Member States, and it is for them to determine the conditions under which legal gender recognition is granted.
The protection and promotion of the rights of the child is a core EU objective. In accordance with Article 24 of the Charter, which guarantees the protection of the rights of the child by the EU institutions and by Member States when they implement EU law, the child’s best interests must be a primary consideration in all matters concerning them, and have the right to express their views freely, with those views taken into account in accordance with their age and maturity[5]. The EU Strategy on the Rights of the Child[6] promotes a rights-based, inclusive and participatory approach, ensuring that every child enjoys the same rights and be able to live free of discrimination, recrimination or intimidation of any kind.
Finally, the right to gather peacefully is a fundamental right to be ensured across the EU. It is enshrined in the Charter and a core element of our democracies.
[1] Lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, non-binary, intersex and queer.
[2] https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/b4952371-4308-47ad-b995-02c539b75dda_en?filename=JUST_template_comingsoon_standard.pdf.
[3] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/char_2012/oj/eng.
[4] https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/5100c375-87e8-40e3-85b5-1adc5f556d6d_en?filename=lgbtiq_strategy_2020-2025_en.pdf.
[5] In line with article 12 of the United Nations’ Convention on the Rights of the Child - https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/convention-rights-child.
[6] https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/rights-child/eu-strategy-rights-child-and-european-child-guarantee_en#the-eu-strategy-on-the-rights-of-the-child.
notes: Asks: does Commission consider children capable of deciding on their gender, given Art 24 Charter reference. Earlier answer: LGBTIQ strategy 2026-2030 adopted; legal gender recognition conditions are Member State competence; Art 24 best interests and views per age/maturity; not covered: explicit position on children's capacity to decide gender.

new_question:

earlier_answer:

new_question:

The Court of Justice of the European Union has ruled that extraditions must be halted if there is a real risk of fundamental rights violations.
1. Will the Commission propose an EU-wide suspension of all extraditions to Hungary under the EAW, given the systemic risks to fundamental rights?
2. Will the Commssion take measures to protect non-EU nationals in the EU, including vulnerable individuals such as refugees, from extradition to Hungary?
3. Is the Commission in contact with the German Government or other German authorities regarding Maja T.’s return, and is it taking any action or is it aware of precedents for reversing an extradition under similar circumstances?

[2] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html.
earlier_answer:
1. The Commission is aware of the case of Maja T. However, the European arrest warrant (EAW) is an entirely judicial procedure between judicial authorities in the Member States based on the particular circumstances of each individual case where surrender is requested. Neither the Commission nor the Member States’ governments can interfere or influence decisions taken by the judicial authorities.
2. The Member States’ authorities are under the obligation to comply with the comprehensive case law on the EAW regarding detention conditions and fair trial rights[1], including on the provision of assurances[2].
The Commission is closely monitoring the transposition into national law of the Framework Decision on EAW, including in Hungary and Germany for which it has launched infringement proceedings pursuant to Article 258 Treaty on the Functioning of the EU. Since 2020, the Commission has issued 26 letters of formal notice concerning the incomplete and incorrect transposition of the Framework Decision on EAW and has taken further steps by way of additional letters of formal notice and reasoned opinions in 2023 and 2024.
3. Indeed, on 8 December 2022, the Commission adopted a Recommendation on the procedural rights of suspects and accused in pre-trial detention and on material detention conditions[3]. It should be noted that the minimum standards, as laid down in the Recommendation, are not legally binding on Member States[4]. Member States should have informed the Commission on their follow-up to this Recommendation by 1 October 2024[5]. Based on this information, the Commission will monitor and assess the measures taken by Member States and aims to submit a report in the course of 2025.

[2] As regards assurances, the CJEU has clarified in Case C-220/18 PPU, ML, that an assurance provided by the issuing Member State - in accordance with Article 15(2) and (3) of the Framework Decision on EAW - that the person concerned, irrespective of the prison he is detained in in the issuing Member State, will not suffer inhuman or degrading treatment on account of the actual and precise conditions of his detention is a factor which the executing judicial authority cannot disregard.
[3] https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_22_7570

new_question:
Long-term crisis in the Greek national health system
Greece’s national health system (the ESY) is in a dire state. A WHO report revealed that the country has one of the highest rates of unmet medical needs (21.9 %). Almost one in five Greeks will not receive the treatment they need due to high costs, poor organisation or systemic incapacity.
But even when access to treatment is possible, the consequences for Greek households are no less devastating. Around a third of low-income households in Greece go bankrupt as a result of the costs necessary medical treatments.
Despite this difficult situation, government policy has left the health system depleted and stagnating. The budget allocated to health remains low and has been further reduced. Brain drain and rising inequality signal a worrying trend for the future of the ESY.
In view of the Commission’s objectives of improving healthcare provision and ensuring a high level of human health for all European citizens, can the Commission say:
1. What tools and initiatives could be used to address the ESY’s systemic failures and mismanagement?
2. How does it intend to investigate the proper use of the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF - NextGenerationEU), the NSRFs and the European Social Fund in the ESY?
3. Does it still have the necessary support instruments to reform the ESY, ensure quality services and fight corruption, or does it limit its role to mere financing without any checks?
earlier_answer:
According to Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union[1], Member States are responsible for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care, including the management thereof and the allocation of the resources assigned to them.
In 2020, 2022 and 2023, Greece received country-specific recommendations to ensure adequate and equal access to healthcare, notably for primary healthcare. They were reflecting, among others, the share of the surveyed population reporting forgone medical needs for financial reasons (9% in 2024)[2]. The situation is worse for women and for lower income groups. Without prejudice to these national responsibilities, the grant component of the Greek Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP) includes reforms and investments, with an estimated cost of EUR 1,537 million[3], to improve the resilience, accessibility, and sustainability of the healthcare system. The national public health prevention programme in particular aims to improve the quality of life of the population and enhance the resilience of the health system by ultimately reducing behavioural risk factors.
Additionally, around EUR 280 million (EU allocation) has been allocated under the European Regional Development Fund to co-finance infrastructure and equipment at all levels of care in the Greek national health system[4]. Moreover, around EUR 250 million are allocated by the European Social Fund Plus towards investments to improve the accessibility and effectiveness of Greek primary healthcare services[5].
All these financial measures are expected to lead to improved health services in Greece and support the principle of equal access to health services, efficiency and social cohesion.

earlier_answer:
When Member States extend the application of national law implementing EU law to situations falling outside the scope of EU law, they must do it in a way that does not undermine or circumvent the application of harmonised rules or obligations under EU law.

Moreover, it needs to be complementary to the existing avenues to access asylum and cannot prevent the aims and objectives of EU law in this field, nor prejudice the rights and guarantees that persons in these situations must be afforded by Member States.

new_question:

earlier_answer:

Member States have between 12 and 36 months to implement the projects (including the organisation of the tenders) as per the grants signed in fourth quarter of 2022. The guidance specifically underlines the importance to reflect the security requirements in the selection and award criteria, and that such should prevail over other criteria such as price. This legal framework will enhance the level of security of products placed on the EU market, including those used in customs. Additionally, the development of standards will foster the competitiveness of our industries by establishing common technical specifications that can reduce both manufacturing costs and time to market.

More than 16 % of the invoices that were examined declared the settlement goods to be of Israeli origin in order to obtain preferential tariff treatment under the EU-Israel Association Agreement, which included goods worth EUR 13.1 million that were ineligible for such treatment.
The report found that even where preferential treatment is correctly denied by EU customs, the Israeli Government reimburses exporters, with at least EUR 63 million disbursed between 2005 and 2024. This compensation scheme renders the EU differentiation ineffective, even under full enforcement.
1. What information does the Commission have about Israel’s compensation scheme for settlement exporters and has it assessed its impact on the EU differentiation policy?
2. Can the Commission confirm whether Israeli customs authorities continue to claim preferential treatment for settlement products and to declare them as being of Israeli origin?
3. Given that differentiation is neutralised by the exporter compensation scheme, how will the Commission ensure an effective trade policy that is consistent with international law? To that end, will the Commission propose a trade measure to prohibit the import of settlement products into the EU?

earlier_answer:
Under the EU-Israel Association Agreement, products manufactured in Israeli settlements located within the territories brought under Israeli administration since June 1967 are not eligible for preferential tariff treatment[1].
Since 1 February 2005, the exclusion of settlement goods from preferential treatment has been implemented in the EU as follows:
- In accordance with a 'Technical Arrangement' concluded by the EU and Israel, the postal code and the name of the city, village or industrial zone where production conferring originating status has taken place are to appear on all proofs of preferential origin issued or made out in Israel.
- Member States' customs authorities check whether the postal codes appearing on Israeli proofs of origin presented to them correspond to any of the postal codes appearing in the list of non-eligible locations made available to them by the Commission and refuse preference where such is the case.
An integrated Tariff of the European Union’s (TARIC) code is needed in the import declaration to confirm that the postal code appearing in the proof of origin corresponds to an eligible location. The Association Agreement provides mechanisms for Member States’ customs to check the correctness of the preferential origin declared. However, the Commission does not collect systematically information on goods entering the EU from Israeli settlements via the Customs Surveillance system[2].

[2] https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/online-services/online-services-and-databases-customs/surveillance-system_en.

new_question:
Tasers cause the death of a person at the hands the police in Torremolinos
On Sunday 7 December 2025, Haitam died of a heart attack after being subdued by eight national police officers in Torremolinos. He was hit by Tasers - which can deliver up to 1 200 volts - at least three times. Images of the scene show police officers immobilising him and threating to taser him again, while cries of pain can be heard. International bodies, including the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture, warn that electroshock weapons can cause death if used repeatedly or for prolonged immobilisation.
In the past year, at least four other racialised people have died in police action, revealing a pattern of racist police violence. This constitutes a breach by Spain of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and of the obligation to ensure proportional and accountable policing, as the Commission highlights in its rule of law reports.
In light of the above:
1. Does the Commission intend to ask the Spanish Government to provide explanations for those deaths?
2. Does it plan to specifically examine the use of Tasers by Member States’ police forces?
3. Does it intend to promote, at EU level, limitations on, or the ban of, Tasers, as well as greater obligations to monitor the use of force?
earlier_answer:
As set out in its reply to previous written questions[1], the Commission condemns any disproportionate use of force or violence. Any use of force by law enforcement authorities must always be proportionate and controlled. Member States should promote and respect their law enforcement rules in full respect of their obligations regarding fundamental rights, as resulting from national law and international human rights commitments. National authorities must investigate individual cases of reported police brutality and ensure that justice is served.
Furthermore, the application of rules in respect of demonstrations, and measures taken by national authorities, including police officers, for the purpose of maintaining law and order and safeguarding internal security, inclusive of those taken on grounds of public policy, are the Member States’ responsibility[2].
The general regime of conditionality for the protection of the EU budget established by Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2020/2092[3], applies to breaches of the principles of the rule of law in a Member State that affect or seriously risk affecting the sound financial management of the EU budget or the protection of the financial interests of the EU in a sufficiently direct way. The Commission does not have any indication to suggest that the conditions to apply Regulation 2020/2092 would be met in this case.

new_question:
Bluetongue epidemic - challenges facing sheep farmers in Portugal
Sheep farming in Portugal has been severely hit by the bluetongue virus epidemic, which, according to the National Confederation of Agricultural Cooperatives and Agricultural Credit of Portugal, ‘has wiped out thousands of sheep across the country and could spread to bovine animals’.
According to the National Confederation of Agriculture (CNA), ‘data from the system on the collection of the cadavers of animals that die on farms (SIRCA) show that the disease is out of control and containment measures are needed right away’.
There are also concerns that SIRCA could collapse.
Both bodies are calling for an immediate and free vaccination campaign and for extraordinary support to cover animal losses, as well as treatment and prevention costs, given that the costs arising from this situation are beyond the means of the vast majority of farms.
As farmers face an unanticipated decline in livestock numbers, the CNA is also warning about the risk of them being penalised by the blanket application of rules under the common agricultural policy (CAP).

2. Will it allow measures adapting the CAP rules to avoid penalising farmers affected by a decline in livestock numbers?
earlier_answer:
1. Infection with bluetongue virus (BTV) is a disease regulated by Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on transmissible animal diseases[1]. Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/1882[2] categorises BTV as a category C disease, and hence, it is subject to optional eradication by Member States. The decision to eradicate the disease and vaccinate may vary by Member State; therefore, the Commission is not planning to launch an EU vaccination campaign.
As a disease subject to optional eradication, EU funding for BTV, including vaccination, is not envisaged for 2024 nor for 2025 to 2027 for BTV eradication programmes in accordance with EU rules[3], neither for BTV emergency measures given that financial resources are allocated to the control and eradication of other major priority animal diseases.
2. Outbreaks of BTV are notifiable through the EU Animal Disease Information System[4] making the Commission and competent authorities aware of the disease situation in order to take the relevant measures to prevent the spread of the disease. The situation is also regularly discussed, including in the Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed[5]. All these actions ensure coordination between the Commission and the Member States.
3. There is a Union legal framework to control BTV, including measures applicable to the movement of animals within the EU[6]. Movements to other Member States must be safe and the animals must either come from free zones or comply with risk mitigation measures (vaccination and others) and certification providing for safe movement. Adequate implementation of the legal framework is the responsibility of the competent authorities of the Member States that may be subject to audits conducted by the Commission.

new_question:
Follow-up on Oberbank’s decision to stop providing cash services and possible action by the Commission
The Commissioner for Economy and Productivity and for Implementation and Simplification, Valdis Dombrovskis, replied to Written Question [REF][1] regarding Oberbank’s withdrawal of cash services stating that the Euro Legal Tender Experts Group (ELTEG) ‘concluded that these solutions do not relieve banks from their social role to provide adequate cash services’ and ‘whether a decision by a credit institution not to provide cash services to their clients is in line with EU law (and the national law transposing EU law) needs to be assessed in each individual case and is a responsibility of the national competent authorities, which the Commission will contact to clarify the situation’.
In the light of this:
1. Has the Commission engaged with the Austrian (and/or other) authorities yet to determine whether Oberbank’s decision to stop providing cash services is compatible with EU goals (proposed cash regulation[2]), treaties and legislation?
2. If so, what were the exact results of this interaction? If not, why not, given the aforementioned reply from the Commissioner?
[1] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html.
[2] Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on the legal tender of euro banknotes and coins.
earlier_answer:
Euro cash has legal tender status in the EU[1]. In its proposal on the legal tender of euro banknotes and coins[2], the Commission emphasizes the need to ensure sufficient and effective access to cash, as without it, citizens cannot use cash for payments and its legal tender status would be undermined. For the same reason, access to various cash services should be ensured, in particular cash withdrawals and cash deposits on payment accounts of credit institutions.
Pending the entry into force of the regulation, the Commission expects Member States to abide by the principles set out in the final report of the 3rd Euro Legal Tender Experts Group[3]. While non-binding, these principles were endorsed by all Member States. The principles emphasise that measures should be taken, where appropriate, that ensure that credit institutions holding payments accounts for citizens and businesses continue to provide essential banking services throughout the euro area. Furthermore, while other possible channels for cash withdrawals and deposits outside the banking sector, such as cash-back in shop, have the potential to complement the cash services of banks, their inherent limitations exclude that they could work as a replacement of ATM networks or cash services at bank branches. Therefore, ELTEG concluded that these solutions do not relieve banks from their social role to provide adequate cash services to citizens and business customers, with the needed geographical coverage.
To ensure financial inclusion, Article 16(1) of the Payment Accounts Directive (PAD)[4] requires Member States to ensure that all credit institutions or a sufficient number of credit institutions offer payment accounts with basic features (PABF) to consumers. Article 17 establishes a list of services that need to be provided for a PABF, including services enabling cash withdrawals[5]. On the basis of the information available to the Commission, the relevant national law transposing PAD requires that all credit institutions that offer payment accounts to consumers have to offer payment accounts with basic features. Whether a decision by a credit institution not to provide cash services to their clients is in line with EU law (and the national law transposing EU law) needs to be assessed in each individual case and is a responsibility of the national competent authorities, which the Commission will contact to clarify the situation.
[1] Article 128 (1) TFEU lays down the legal tender status of euro banknotes, and article 11 of Regulation EC/974/98 does so with regard to euro coins.
[2] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52023PC0364.
[3] https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/expert-groups-register/screen/expert-groups/consult?lang=en&groupId=3754&fromMembers=true&memberType=4&memberId=93719.
[4] Directive 2014/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 July 2014 on the comparability of fees related to payment accounts, payment account switching and access to payment accounts with basic features (OJ L 257, 28.8.2014, p. 214, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2014/92/oj).
[5] Article 17(1) point c refers to ‘services enabling cash withdrawals within the EU from a payment account at the counter or at automated teller machines during or outside the credit institution’s opening hours.
