new_question:
Lack of legal remedy in the event of failure to make a referral and to comply with the obligation to state reasons pursuant to CILFIT and Remling - follow-up question to [REF] and [REF]
In its answers to questions for written answer [REF][1] and [REF][2], the Commission did not provide a clear answer to the question of whether the absence of a judicial remedy against a wrongful failure to refer is compatible with Article 19(1) of the Treaty on European Union (TEU) and Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (CFR). According to the CILFIT judgment (Case C-283/81), a court of final instance is exempt from the obligation to refer a question for a preliminary ruling under Article 267(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) only in exceptional circumstances. According to the Remling judgment (Case C-767/23), the court must provide specific and concrete reasons for the non-referral.
1. Does the Commission consider the absence of a legal remedy before a specialised court in the event of a breach of these obligations to be compatible with Article 19(1) TEU and Article 47 CFR, and if so, on what basis under EU law?
2. If not, what specific requirements does this entail for the Member States?
3. If the Commission does not systematically record infringements of the obligations to refer and to state reasons for non-referral set out in the CILFIT and Remling judgments, how can it possibly identify any structural deficits or systematic breaches as referred to in its previous replies?
[1] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_DE.html.
[2] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_DE.html.
earlier_answer:
Article 267 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) sets up a dialogue between the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) and the courts of the Member States, in which the latter are closely involved in the uniform interpretation and correct application of EU law and the protection of individual rights.
In its recent judgment of 24 March 2026[1], the Court of Justice recalled that a national court or tribunal of last instance is subject to an obligation to make a reference for a preliminary ruling, of which it may be relieved only in three situations: lack of relevance of the question of EU law raised, where the EU law at issue had already been interpreted by the Court of Justice or where that interpretation of EU law is so obvious as to leave no scope for any reasonable doubt of the national court. The Court of Justice further held that a national court or tribunal of last instance must give in all cases, specifically and concretely, the reasons why one of these exceptions applies when refusing to refer questions for a preliminary ruling.
The Commission monitors structural deficits in the dialogue under Article 267 TFEU. As guardian of the Treaties, the Commission may initiate infringement proceedings under Article 258 TFEU for possible non-compliance with Article 267(3) TFEU when a Member State adopts legislation preventing proper judicial cooperation under that provision, or when evidence shows a systematic breach.
[1] C-767/23 - Remling.
notes: Asks: Q1 is lack of remedy for wrongful non-referral compatible with Art 19(1) TEU/Art 47 CFR; Q2 requirements for MS if not; Q3 how structural deficits identified without recording breaches. Earlier answer: Art 267 dialogue; Remling (24 Mar 2026) three CILFIT exceptions and duty to state reasons; monitors structural deficits, infringement possible; not covered: Q1 remedy compatibility, Q2, Q3 method.

The Council of the European Union adopted subsequently far-reaching restrictive measures, including in particular the freezing of funds and economic resources of numerous Russian entities and individuals, as well as prohibitions, among others, to provide support to entities established in Russia with over 50 percent public ownership or control. Funding of European Citizen’s Initiative My Voice, My Choice
In response to written questions about the funding of the European citizens’ initiative entitled ‘Funding of European Citizen’s Initiative My Voice, My Choice’[1], Commissioner Hadja Lahbib indicated that Zavod Raziskovalni inštitut 8. marec, an initiator of and donor to My Voice, My Choice, was the only organisation in receipt of EU funding to foster civic participation among youth and civil society. The Commission states that no other donors to My Voice, My Choice received EU funding. In the light of this response:
1. Will the Commission make the grant agreement and annexes related to the EU funding granted to Zavod Raziskovalni inštitut 8. marec public and clarify what kind of civic participation projects it carried out as a result of the EU funding?
2. Can the Commission guarantee that these funds were not used to finance My Voice, My Choice?
3. Considering that the Commission funds pro-abortion organisations the International Planned Parenthood Federation and the European Women’s Lobby, organisations which in turn distribute part of such funding to their partners across the EU, can the Commission clarify if any such funding was used to support My Voice, My Choice?
[1] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html.
earlier_answer:
Regulation (EU) 2019/788[1] on the European Citizens’ Initiative (ECI) provides for rules on transparency from the group of organisers on the sources of funding.
Based on the information published[2] by the organisers of the said ECI, the sources of funding are available for transparency and accountability. Amongst its listed sponsors, only the Zavod Raziskovalni inštitut 8. marec is a beneficiary of EU funding[3].

new_question:
Pandemic risks from gain-of-function research
Robert Ray Redfield Jr., former head of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), was responsible for their management during the COVID-19 pandemic. After initial analyses, Redfield concluded in 2021 that SARS-CoV-2 was likely to have originated from a laboratory in Wuhan (lab-leak hypothesis) and not from natural transmission from animals to humans[1].[2] He stressed that the virus was transmitted unusually efficiently from person to person, making natural formation unlikely. Redfield particularly criticised gain-of-function research on high-risk viruses, funded by, among others, the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the US State Department, the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and the US Department of Defence[3]. He said that such research had so far not prevented any pandemic, but may instead have contributed to the biggest pandemic in modern history. Following his hearing, the US House of Representatives unanimously voted in favour of a draft law requiring intelligence services to disclose information on the origin of SARS-CoV-2[4].
1. Where in the EU is gain-of-function research carried out and what exactly is being researched there?
2. Is it ethically justifiable to manipulate viruses with pandemic potential if the benefits are scientifically unproven?
3. What is the Commission’s view of the origin of the COVID-19 virus and what scientific evidence is this view based on?
[1] https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-023-00701-1.
[2] https://oversight.house.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/2023.03.08-Statement-of-Dr.-Robert-R-Redfield88.pdf.
[3] https://mein-stuttgart.com/us-steuerzahler-dollars-haben-zur-groessten-pandemie-beigetragen-die-unsere-welt-gesehen-hat/.
[4] https://www.cbsnews.com/news/us-government-agencies-may-have-been-double-billed-projects-wuhan-china-records-indicate-probe/.
earlier_answer:
Gain-of-function research involves genetically altering an organism to enhance its biological functions and is undertaken to better understand diseases and develop therapies and vaccines. The potential risks associated with creating more infectious or deadly pathogens need to be carefully managed and weighed against the benefits for public health.
The Commission’s approach to protection from potential biological weapons is guided by the 2017 Action Plan to enhance preparedness against chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear (CBRN) security risks[1].
In this context, the Commission established the Customs Crisis Management function, enabling rapid response by customs authorities to security risks stemming from EU imports, including potential biological weapons. This mechanism has been activated in past crises such as the COVID-19 pandemic.
The support to gain-of-function research is possible under the EU research and innovation framework programme[2], subject to strict eligibility criteria and ethical conditions, verified through a scientific and ethical evaluation and screening of proposals and projects raising ethical issues, and where appropriate a security check. The programme has supported gain-of-function research on influenza virus to improve the response to emerging infectious diseases[3].
The Commission will continue to implement the highest levels of ethics integrity in the research and innovation domain, and to protect in this context EU values and security.
[1] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52017DC0610.
[2] Regulation (EU) 2021/695 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 28 April 2021 establishing Horizon Europe - the Framework Programme for Research and Innovation, laying down its rules for participation and dissemination, and repealing Regulations (EU) No 1290/2013 and (EU) No 1291/2013.
[3] Horizon 2020 COMPARE project carried out at Erasmus Medical Centre, Rotterdam in the Netherlands: Collaborative Management Platform for detection and Analyses of (Re-)emerging and foodborne outbreaks in Europe (2014-2019; https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/643476).
notes: Asks: Q1 where EU gain-of-function research occurs and what is researched; Q2 whether manipulating viruses with pandemic potential is ethically justifiable when benefits are scientifically unproven; Q3 the Commission’s view on COVID-19’s origin and its scientific evidence. Earlier answer: EU research funding is subject to eligibility and ethics checks and, where appropriate, security checks; H2020 COMPARE supported influenza research at Erasmus MC in Rotterdam (Q1 example); risks must be weighed against public-health benefits (Q2); not covered: a comprehensive account of research locations and subjects, the ethical question under the stated premise, and Q3.

new_question:
Larco must be supported and modernised and all workers rehired
The New Democracy government is moving full speed ahead with its dangerous plans to close mining company Larco and take jobs away following the rejection of the application for interim measures, which was submitted by workers who were asking to keep their jobs.
Larco is a strategically important business due to the high natural, material and technical value of its infrastructure and the fact that it is the only company in the EU with domestically owned nickel and cobalt deposits.
A premeditated crime for which New Democracy bears responsibility and which is taking place with the complicity of all previous governments (Syriza and Pasok), is being committed on the pretext that Larco is allegedly a financial drain on the Greek State. Everyone contributed to the process of discrediting and undermining the company’s capabilities through the government’s ‘liquidation while in operation’ plan.
In view of this, what is the Commission’s position concerning:
1. Larco employees’ call for the company to become operational again and for all of its existing experienced staff to be hired back, with no layoffs?
2. The fact that the only nickel and cobalt deposits and the only pyrometallurgical plant in the EU are being sold off chiefly because of the EU’s ‘green and digital transition’ strategy, prioritising profit and the competitiveness of business groups?
3. The fact that the government’s claim that the company is a financial drain comes also in the context of the outrageous fine for breach of State aid rules, which was ordered by the European Court of Justice following the Commission’s referral?
earlier_answer:
1.+2. As the Commission referred in its answers to written questions [REF], [REF], [REF], [REF] and [REF], on 27 March 2014, the Commission adopted a decision ordering Greece to recover aid of EUR 135 million (plus interest) granted to LARCO in the form of State guarantees and capital injections in the period 2008-2010.
To date, the unlawful and incompatible State aid has not been repaid. Greece is still under the obligation to recover that aid.
LARCO has been placed under special administration in 2020. According to the information available to the Commission, the sale of LARCO’s assets in the context of its special administration is ongoing. After such sale, the new owner(s) could potentially mine laterite and produce ferronickel in the sold facilities, employing possibly new and/or former LARCO employees and would not be liable for the recovery of the incompatible aid if there is economic discontinuity between LARCO and the new owner(s) of the assets.
3. [1] Judgment of 9 November 2017, Commission v Greece, C-481/16, ECLI:EU:C:2017:845.
notes: Asks: Q1 reopen Larco and rehire all experienced staff without layoffs; Q2 the sale of its nickel and cobalt deposits and plant in relation to the green and digital transition; Q3 the State aid recovery and court penalties. new_question:
Urgent need to take measures at European level to combat shrinkflation
For the past two years, consumers have been faced with a prolonged cost-of-living crisis due to the explosion of inflation, skyrocketing prices and a significant reduction in their buying power. At the same time, there has been a Europe-wide spread in the phenomenon of reduced size or quantity of products sold in the same packaging, with prices remaining the same or, more commonly, increasing (shrinkflation). Such practices increase the real cost of products, are not easily noticed by consumers, and aggravate still further the cost-of-living crisis in which millions of citizens throughout Europe find themselves. In the absence of an effective European framework for protecting consumers against escalating shrinkflation, some countries are taking, or preparing to take, national measures to combat it[1].
In view of this:
1. Does the Commission consider shrinkflation to be a misleading commercial practice[2]?
2. Does it intend to take steps to combat this phenomenon, including amendment of the regulation on provision of consumer information on foods[3], so that it will be compulsory to indicate cases of shrinkflation on product packaging?
3. What measures can national governments take to combat this phenomenon?
[1] https://www.just-food.com/news/france-seeks-eu-approval-for-shrinkflation-move/?cf-view, https://www.retailbrew.com/stories/2023/09/29/germany-drafting-anti-shrinkflation-law
[2] Article 6 of Directive 2005/29/EC, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EL/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32005L0029.
[3] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/1169/2018-01-01?locale=el
earlier_answer:
The Commission adopted[1] a proposal for a new Regulation on Packaging and Packaging Waste on 30 November 2022 that contains a number of measures to address, inter alia, packaging minimisation. Article 9 of the proposal requires that the empty space of packaging shall be reduced to the minimum necessary for ensuring its functionality, in relation to the total volume of the packaged product and its characteristics and also considering the material the packaging is made of. The proposal defines performance criteria that consider product protection, manufacturing processes, logistics, information, hygiene and safety and outlines a methodology for determination of the minimum packaging volume and weight.
As regards consumer protection, the Price Indication Directive[2], the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive[3] (UCPD), the Consumer Rights Directive[4] and sector-specific legislation, where applicable, require traders to indicate the total price of a product and its main characteristics, such as size or quantity, without limiting the traders’ freedom to set retail prices or to determine the size or quantity of their products. UCPD prohibits misleading commercial practices, including misleading overall presentation of the product that causes or is likely to cause the consumers to take transactional decisions they would not have taken otherwise. The Food Information to Consumers Regulation[5] requires that the net quantity of foods has to be indicated on the label. The enforcement of EU consumer law falls under the competence of Member States which carry out market surveillance to assess and put an end to these practices. Consumers are encouraged to report such practices to their Member State authorities.
[1] https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_22_7155
[2] Directive 98/6/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 February 1998 on consumer protection in the indication of the prices of products offered to consumers, OJ L 80, 18.3.1998, p. 27.
[3] Directive 2005/29/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 May 2005 concerning unfair business-to-consumer commercial practices, OJ L 149, 11.6.2005, p 22.
[4] Directive 2011/83/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 201 on consumer rights, OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 64.
[5] Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2011 on the provision of food information to consumers, amending Regulations (EC) No 1924/2006 and (EC) No 1925/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council, and repealing Commission Directive 87/250/EEC, Council Directive 90/496/EEC, Commission Directive 1999/10/EC, Directive 2000/13/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council, Commission Directives 2002/67/EC and 2008/5/EC and Commission Regulation (EC) No 608/2004, OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 18.
notes: Asks: Q1 is shrinkflation misleading; Q2 EU action incl. mandatory FIC labelling; Q3 national measures. Earlier answer: PPWR packaging minimisation; UCPD bans misleading presentation, price/quantity indication, FIC net quantity (Q1, Q2 general); enforcement by Member States (Q3); not covered: shrinkflation label amendment.

new_question:
Review of potential EU funding for Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte
Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (GFF) is an association in Germany that was set up in 2015 and purports to defend supposed fundamental rights. Cases are selected specifically to bring about wide-reaching legal decisions. The association submits constitutional complaints, prepares expert opinions and runs media campaigns. While it describes itself as non-partisan, the choice of topics and the patterns of arguments used are anchored in an ideological, liberal-progressive fundamental rights discourse.
The organisation’s inconspicuous mask recently slipped. It openly acts as an arm of anti-democratic forces, which use any means necessary to impose a ban on the party leading every opinion poll: Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). To that end, an expert report is currently being prepared, for which former AfD politicians have also been approached to encourage them to make statements criticising the party or provide internal information and documents. In doing so, the organisation does not act as an independent association, but rather as an active political actor that uses rule of law procedures as a pretext to undermine the democratic representation of a large portion of the population.
In view of these developments, it must be ensured that organisations that have such an anti-democratic agenda do not have access to EU funding.
1. Has GFF ever applied for or received EU funding, including indirect funding by way of third-party organisations?
2. What mechanisms are in place to ensure that EU funds do not go to organisations that seek to undermine democratic processes or restrict the people’s political representation?
earlier_answer:
Neither the Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte nor the European AI & Society Fund are beneficiaries of EU funding.
The Digital Freedom Fund is the beneficiary of an EU grant for the implementation of project DIGIRISE, ‘Developing Information, Guidance, and Interconnectedness for (Charter) Rights Integration in Strategies for Enforcement’[1]. The project has been selected under the call CERV-2022-CHAR-LITI[2] to ‘promote capacity building and awareness on the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights[3] and activities on strategic litigation relating to democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights breaches’.
The objectives of the project are to raise awareness of the Charter’s relevance for protecting digital rights and to improve knowledge of judicial pathways to enforce digital Charter rights.
Through annual calls for proposals, the Commission funds projects to support civil society and other relevant actors in raising awareness on the Charter, which is binding primary EU law. The eligibility and award criteria are specified in the call documents. The projects are selected by independent experts. Under the ethics criteria, all funded projects are required to comply with the founding values of the EU as set out in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union and with Article 21 of the Charter.
The project does not foresee the possibility of redistributing EU funding to third parties.
[1] DIGIRISE - Digital Freedom Fund: https://digitalfreedomfund.org/digirise-2/.
[2] Call for proposals CERV-2022-CHAR-LITI - Commission: https://www.eacea.ec.europa.eu/call-proposals-cerv-2022-char-liti_en.
[3] Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, OJ C 326, 26.10.2012, p. 391-407.
notes: Asks: Q1 has GFF applied for/received EU funds, incl. indirect; Q2 safeguards against funding anti-democratic orgs. Earlier answer: GFF not an EU beneficiary (Q1, direct); Digital Freedom Fund CERV grant, no third-party redistribution; independent selection, Art 2 TEU ethics criteria (Q2); not covered: whether GFF ever applied.

Russia - part 2

1. Can the Commission indicate how much money - with a breakdown of the figures per Member State and per year - Member States have paid directly or indirectly to Russia for energy imports since February 2022 (including transmission fees paid in third countries), and if not, why not?

[1] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html.
earlier_answer:
As clearly stated by the European Leaders in the Versailles Declaration in March 2022, and in line with the REPowerEU Plan, the European Union aims to fully phase out Russian fossil fuels. On 6 May 2025 the Commission adopted a roadmap[1] towards fully ending Russian energy imports in a coordinated, gradual and secure manner, supporting Member States in stepping up and accelerating efforts in that direction.
Based on Eurostat’s trade statistics[2], Member States paid to Russia EUR 21,6 billion in 2024 as compared to EUR 144 billion in 2022. This 85% decline in payments translates into savings of EUR 122 billion, underscoring the EU’s progress in reducing its dependence on Russian energy imports. To achieve this, the measures under the REPowerEU and the EU's sanctions regime, promoting inter-alia domestically produced renewable energy, energy efficiency and supply diversification have been paramount. All Russian pipeline gas imports, but those coming via the Turkstream, have halted.
As regards external policies, between February 2022 and December 2024 payments to Russia amounted to approximately EUR 3,5 million under contracts concluded prior to 2021 and providing support through direct management for civil society and independent media. Regarding internal policies, less than EUR 30,000 were paid to Russian entities during the same period.
[1] https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_25_1131.
[2] https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ds-045409__custom_15257993/default/table?lang=en.

new_question:
PFAS rules and public health
The Clean Industry Pact included the adoption of measures for the chemicals industry by the end of 2025. It is also an important public health issue, not least because those measures will cover PFAS.
In late March 2025, a meeting involving members of the Commission and a number of stakeholders was held on the topic[1]. Impact on health was also discussed (how to protect human health and the environment from toxic chemicals, including ongoing work on PFAS). Stéphane Séjourné and Jessika Roswall appear to be the only commissioners to have taken part in that meeting.
Could the Commission please answer the following questions in this regard:
1. How are DG SANTE departments and the Commissioner for Health involved in preparatory work for measures in the Chemical Industry Package and PFAS in particular?
2. What proposals has the Commissioner for Health made to Commissioners Séjourné and Roswall to reduce the impact of PFAS on public health and limit the European population’s exposure to PFAS in the future?
[1] EU Reporter article, 25 March 2025, ‘Commission hosts a high-level meeting on the upcoming Chemicals Industry Package’
earlier_answer:
The Commission would like to recall that the EU legislation on plant protection products[1] (Regulation (EC) 1107/2009) is among the strictest in the world. Only active substances which have no harmful effects on human health and no unacceptable effects on the environment can be approved for use in plant protection products (PPP) and Member States can only authorise plant protection products if they also fulfil these conditions.
In the restriction proposal related to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) under the REACH Regulation[2], the four Member States and Norway who submitted the proposal[3] did indeed exempt active substances used in PPP as they considered that Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, which requires a full risk assessment before approval of active substances, should address the concern of PFAS used in PPP.
In fact, for each active substance, including also those that are PFAS, it is assessed whether the substance or its metabolites are persistent and whether they are bioaccumulating and/or toxic. Active substances that are persistent, bioaccumulating and toxic, or very persistent and very bioaccumulating cannot be approved. The Commission has recently initiated an exchange of views with Member States in order to understand if there are already discussions in place at national level for active substances that are identified as PFAS but nevertheless meet the current approval criteria in Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009.
[1] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2009/1107/oj
[2] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:02006R1907-20221217
[3] https://echa.europa.eu/-/echa-publishes-pfas-restriction-proposal
notes: Asks: Q1 DG SANTE/Health Commissioner role in Chemicals Industry Package and PFAS; Q2 Health Commissioner's PFAS proposals to Sejourne/Roswall. Earlier answer: PPP Regulation 1107/2009, PFAS REACH restriction exempts PPP actives, PBT criteria, talks with Member States; not covered: Q1, Q2, the 2025 package.

new_question:
Review of the COVID-19 vaccine authorisation and support for vaccine injury claimants
Many claims for damages have been filed against vaccine manufacturers. Most recently, a woman brought an action before the Frankfurt Regional Court (judgment of 14 April 2024, case No 2-12 O 264/22)[1]. She claims to have suffered serious side-effects following the vaccine, including constant migraines, mental impairment, heart palpitations and permanent immunodeficiencies. She also reported that her quality of life had deteriorated significantly, pointing to difficulties concentrating, hypercoagulability and heart valve defects - all of which she attributes to the vaccine.
Her claim was dismissed, however, on the grounds that she would have been previously aware of the side-effects. What is more, the ‘binding legal effect of an administrative act’ (the vaccine authorisation in this case) is such that ‘where the relevant administrative authority has issued an effective administrative act expressly authorising a specific conduct - as with an authorisation - the admissibility of said conduct shall not be subject to judicial review by the civil courts until such time as the administrative act has been revoked or otherwise annulled by the relevant authority or an administrative court (Neue Juristische Wocheschrift 2023, 2259)’
1. What measures is the Commission using to support people who can prove personal injury as a result of the COVID-19 vaccine?
2. How is it working together with the Member States to ensure transparent communication and reporting on the side-effects brought on by the COVID-19 vaccine?
3. Does it still stand behind its earlier decision to grant an authorisation for COVID-19 vaccines, even though many side-effects have been reported and the vaccines have not proven to be as effective as the manufacturers promised and the public was made to expect?
[1] https://www.rv.hessenrecht.hessen.de/bshe/document/LARE240000209/part/L.
earlier_answer:
As the Commission pointed out in its reply to written question [REF][1], the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and national authorities evaluate data on reported events in EudraVigilance[2] to determine if there is any signal indicating causality and take action as appropriate. As referred to in the reply to question [REF][3], most suspected side effects recorded in EudraVigilance are not eventually confirmed as causally associated to the medicine administration. The same happened for the COVID-19 vaccines. As mentioned in the reply to question [REF][4], an unprecedented high number of people has been administered COVID-19 vaccines[5] and the number of reported suspected side effects for these vaccines is consequently higher in total numbers. No safety signal for increased mortality with any of the authorised COVID-19 vaccines has been identified by EMA to date.
The Commission has provided full answers to the questions of the Honourable Members related to COVID-19 vaccines, including results from the pharmacovigilance, and has ensured the largest possible transparency both as regards the negotiations it held with companies for the purchase of vaccines and the outcome of those negotiations.
In response to the European Ombudsman’s recommendation of 26 January 2022 regarding the Commission’s refusal of public access to text messages[6], the Commission confirmed the search undertaken by the President’s cabinet for relevant text messages had not yielded any results.
Finally, an action for the annulment of a decision adopted by the Commission under Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001[7] further to a request for public access to the relevant text messages has been brought before the General Court in Case T-36/23[8]. This Case is currently pending.

new_question:

new_question:
Organ donation in Europe
Last year, 2 042 organ donations were made in Italy, while the number of transplants reached 4 462. A total of 13.5 million citizens have recorded their decision to consent to organ donation on the national transplant information system.
Yet, despite the fact that donation rates are continuously rising across Europe, the existing EU legislation on donation and on the exchange of human organs between Member States dates back to 2010 and 2012 respectively.
The sector faces many challenges, from countries having different cultural approaches to donation to there being a lack of proper and comprehensive information on donation and, above all, adequate and effective cooperation between Member States. Meanwhile, more than 50 000 EU citizens are waiting for a transplant.
In view of the above:
1. Does the Commission plan in the near future to set up an integration system for organ donations between Member States?
2. Will it introduce funding for the national bodies that have for years been trying to get things to progress in this area?
3. Does it not see a need to establish a harmonised awareness-raising programme to encourage more people to opt in to being donors in the EU?
earlier_answer:
As the Commission pointed out in its reply to written question [REF], public health is an area where the Union supports, complements or supplements the actions of the Member States (Article 6 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU (TFEU)[1]). The EU’s competence in the field of public health is limited under Article 168 TFEU and as regards organs covers setting standards for quality and safety (Article 168(4)(a) TFEU). The organisation of transplant care does not fall under this mandate, but under the competence of the Member States.
The EU continues to support the sector through funded actions. The Commission also hosts a network that brings transplant authorities and professionals together to discuss common concerns[2], this network has proven very useful during the COVID crisis, which has indeed significantly impacted transplant rates, for example by sharing good practices to strengthen resilience of transplant systems in case of crisis.
The Commission furthermore underlines that several actions developed under the EU Action Plan on Organ Donation and Transplantation 2009-2015 focused on the role of transplant donor coordinators and on the collaboration with intensive care units. Most of these outcomes are still relevant, while Member States implement organisational improvement in their national transplant systems.
Finally, the Commission is planning for support under the EU4Health programme to strengthen EU-level resilience of transplant practices within a (COVID-like) crisis context.
[1] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:12012E/TXT&from=EN
[2] https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/regexpert/index.cfm?do=groupDetail.groupDetail&groupID=1718
notes: Asks: Q1 an integration system for organ donations between Member States; Q2 funding for national bodies; Q3 a harmonised donor awareness programme. Earlier answer: transplant organisation is a Member State competence; the Commission hosts a network of transplant authorities and professionals, supports funded actions and plans EU4Health crisis-resilience support (Q1 and Q2 context); not covered: a planned donation integration system, funding specifically for the national bodies described, and Q3.

new_question:
Security-related concerns regarding current EU customs scanning equipment and the Customs Control Equipment Instrument funds
Both the Draghi report on Europe’s global competitiveness and the new European defence industrial strategy[1] have uncovered significant gaps in Europe’s industrial capacity. These gaps have led to Europe being economically dependent on high-risk non-EU countries. This poses credible threats to the security of the EU and the wider Schengen area. One such threat is Chinese cyber warfare, including espionage and alleged data theft through China-produced scanning equipment at the EU’s external borders.
1. Will the Commission support the development of European ‘champions’ and EU-based partnerships with trusted allies to provide border scanning equipment and services that are controlled and inspected by the EU?
2. Is it the Commission’s view that the Customs Control Equipment Instrument funds could be extended to include defence products, for instance by classifying border scanning equipment as defence-related, and achieving this through transparent award procedures?
3. Will the Commission take steps to ensure that border and customs control scanning equipment is procured solely through transparent public tenders, restricted to EU companies and EU-based partnerships, thereby guaranteeing the security of EU and Schengen area borders as well as cybersecurity?
[1] https://defence-industry-space.ec.europa.eu/eu-defence-industry/edis-our-common-defence-industrial-strategy_en.
earlier_answer:
To date the Commission has not received concrete evidence regarding customs control equipment technical failures compromising the security of the EU or human rights.
As stated in the previous Commission answers to written questions [REF], [REF] and [REF], the responsibility for procurement procedures lies with the Member States. The Customs Control Equipment Instrument (CCEI) eligibility criteria and requirements are specified in the 2021-2022 invitation to submit a proposal and corresponding grant agreements.
As stated in the previous Commission answer to written question [REF], in the current framework, procurement can be restricted by a Member State, in particular following a national security assessment. The security of the equipment is of utmost importance and the Commission provides guidance to the Member States in this regard.
To further protect the security of the EU, the Commission is envisaging additional measures for future CCEI calls. This includes in particular reinforced requirements to ensure the security of the equipment and its use (including the protection of data produced) within the CCEI relevant procurement and the necessity to involve the national security/cybersecurity services in the process when appropriate.
notes: Asks: Q1 support for European scanner providers and partnerships with trusted allies; Q2 extending CCEI funds to defence products through transparent awards; Q3 transparent scanner tenders restricted to EU companies and EU-based partnerships. Earlier answer: procurement is a Member State responsibility and can be restricted following a security assessment; the Commission provides guidance and envisages stronger equipment and data security requirements for future CCEI calls (Q3); not covered: Q1, the proposed CCEI extension in Q2, and the requested EU-wide tender and supplier restrictions in Q3.

new_question:
Closure or termination of numerous bank accounts belonging to clubs, political parties, businesses or private individuals by banks in Germany in particular
As the Commission will already be aware, numerous bank accounts belonging to particular clubs, political parties, companies or individuals have been closed or terminated by banks in Germany[1].
1. Of which specific instances of such account closures or terminations in the EU in the last four months is the Commission aware?
2. Is the Commission ruling out the possibility that this can be traced back, directly or indirectly, to US domestic regulation?
3. Are there US regulations that could indirectly influence EU law and result in bank account closures for clubs, political parties or individuals that are operating lawfully within the EU?
[1] https://taz.de/Alle-Konten-gekuendigt/!6140903/
earlier_answer:
The Commission is aware of the issue of debanking. Credit institutions, like other economic operators, have in principle the freedom to decide with whom they want to enter into a contract or maintain a business relationship. Yet, the Payment Services Directive (PSD)[1] provides certain rules for the termination of payment accounts[2].
To ensure financial inclusion, the Payment Accounts Directive (PAD)[3] provides all EU consumers the right to a payment account with basic features (PABF) and sets out only a limited number of reasons, such as that the opening of the account would lead to an infringement of anti-money laundering rules, which can justify the refusal for opening a PABF. Unilateral closure of a PABF by the bank is also only allowed for limited reasons[4]. A ‘reputational risk’ for the bank or ideological beliefs of the consumer cannot as such justify the closure or refusal to open a PABF.
In order to tackle instances of debanking and following the European Banking Authority (EBA)’s opinion on the scale and impact of de-risking in the EU, the EBA has issued guidelines for credit institutions to facilitate access to financial services and tackle unwarranted de-risking[5]. The new Anti-Money Laundering/Countering the Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT) framework applying from July 2027 requires institutions that decide to terminate a business relationship to keep records of the grounds for such a decision. This will allow supervisors to assess whether institutions have appropriately calibrated their customer due diligence practices. Furthermore, AML supervisors will be required to cooperate with financial supervisors responsible for the PSD and the PAD to reduce de-risking practices.
[1] Article 55 of Directive (EU) 2015/2366 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 November 2015 on payment services in the internal market, amending Directives 2002/65/EC, 2009/110/EC and 2013/36/EU and Regulation (EU) No 1093/2010, and repealing Directive 2007/64/EC (Text with EEA relevance) OJ L 337, 23.12.2015.
[2] In particular, payment service providers are only able to terminate payment accounts if this is provided in a contract and are obliged to give at least a 2- month notice to the client. Moreover, Member States’ laws and regulations governing the rights of the parties to declare the contract unenforceable or void are applicable.
[3] Directive 2014/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 July 2014 on the comparability of fees related to payment accounts, payment account switching and access to payment accounts with basic features Text with EEA relevance.
[4] This includes for example that the consumer is no longer legally resident in the EU or has used the account for illegal purposes.
[5]https://www.eba.europa.eu/sites/default/files/document_library/Publications/Guidelines/2023/1054144/Guidelines%20on%20MLTF%20risk%20management%20and%20access%20to%20financial%20services.pdf.
notes: Asks: Q1 specific account closures in last four months; Q2 link to US regulation; Q3 US rules causing EU debanking. Earlier answer: debanking in general: contractual freedom, PSD termination rules, PAD basic account and limited closure grounds, EBA de-risking guidelines, AML record-keeping from 2027; not covered: Q1 cases, Q2, Q3 US angle.

2. Is the Council in favour of suspending the EU-Israel Association Agreement and imposing an arms embargo, among other measures?

earlier_answer:

The Foreign Affairs Council (FAC) regularly discusses the situation in the Middle East. It has also reaffirmed that its long-standing position on the Middle East Process - as set out in several Council conclusions - is a commitment to achieving a two-state solution with the State of Israel and an independent, democratic, contiguous, sovereign and viable State of Palestine living side-by-side in peace, security and mutual recognition[4], and stressed that a credible pathway to Palestinian statehood is a crucial component of that political process.

PFAS rules and public health
The Clean Industry Pact included the adoption of measures for the chemicals industry by the end of 2025. It is also an important public health issue, not least because those measures will cover PFAS.
In late March 2025, a meeting involving members of the Commission and a number of stakeholders was held on the topic[1]. Impact on health was also discussed (how to protect human health and the environment from toxic chemicals, including ongoing work on PFAS). Stéphane Séjourné and Jessika Roswall appear to be the only commissioners to have taken part in that meeting.

1. How are DG SANTE departments and the Commissioner for Health involved in preparatory work for measures in the Chemical Industry Package and PFAS in particular?
2. What proposals has the Commissioner for Health made to Commissioners Séjourné and Roswall to reduce the impact of PFAS on public health and limit the European population’s exposure to PFAS in the future?
[1] EU Reporter article, 25 March 2025, ‘Commission hosts a high-level meeting on the upcoming Chemicals Industry Package’
earlier_answer:
Although an environmental quality standard (EQS) is set[1] for perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS) as a priority substance in surface waters under the Water Framework Directive[2] and Member States must meet that EQS by 2027, no EQS is set for perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) at EU level. However, Member States must set and meet EQS for substances posing a risk to or via the water environment at national level. The Netherlands had not done so for PFOA when it reported its second river basin management plans.
Given the risks from other per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), the Commission included an EQS for a group of 24 PFAS, including PFOA, in its 2022 proposal to revise the priority substances list[3], which is under negotiation.
The proposal for a Directive on Soil Monitoring and Resilience[4], also under negotiation, would require Member States to identify all sites where soil contamination[5] is suspected, do a risk assessment and take appropriate risk-reduction measures.
Provisions in the proposal[6] on revising the Industrial Emissions Directive[7] and the European Pollutant Release and Transfer Register Regulation[8] would promote the use of safer alternatives to PFAS and improve emissions reporting.
Five national authorities have proposed restricting all PFAS[9] as a group under the Regulation on the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals[10]. The scientific committees of the European Chemicals Agency are preparing an opinion, on the basis of which the Commission will take a decision.
The Commission is committed to strengthening the application of the Polluter Pays Principle in European law[11], and to implementing the Environmental Liability Directive[12], which may be relevant in some PFAS contamination cases.

earlier_answer:

Member States should promote and respect their law enforcement rules in full respect of their European and international human rights obligations. According to EU rules, public authorities are required to take all necessary steps to prevent and punish actions by private individuals that aim to restrict the free movement of goods.

2. Will the Commission ask the French Government to act with the appropriate firmness to restore in practice the rights that economic operators enjoy under the single market?

earlier_answer:
The free movement of goods is one of the four fundamental freedoms of the EU and a cornerstone of the internal market. earlier_answer:

new_question:
Urgent need to take measures at European level to combat shrinkflation
For the past two years, consumers have been faced with a prolonged cost-of-living crisis due to the explosion of inflation, skyrocketing prices and a significant reduction in their buying power. At the same time, there has been a Europe-wide spread in the phenomenon of reduced size or quantity of products sold in the same packaging, with prices remaining the same or, more commonly, increasing (shrinkflation). Such practices increase the real cost of products, are not easily noticed by consumers, and aggravate still further the cost-of-living crisis in which millions of citizens throughout Europe find themselves. In the absence of an effective European framework for protecting consumers against escalating shrinkflation, some countries are taking, or preparing to take, national measures to combat it[1].
In view of this:
1. Does the Commission consider shrinkflation to be a misleading commercial practice[2]?
2. Does it intend to take steps to combat this phenomenon, including amendment of the regulation on provision of consumer information on foods[3], so that it will be compulsory to indicate cases of shrinkflation on product packaging?
3. What measures can national governments take to combat this phenomenon?
[1] https://www.just-food.com/news/france-seeks-eu-approval-for-shrinkflation-move/?cf-view, https://www.retailbrew.com/stories/2023/09/29/germany-drafting-anti-shrinkflation-law
[2] Article 6 of Directive 2005/29/EC, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EL/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32005L0029.
[3] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/1169/2018-01-01?locale=el
earlier_answer:
The Commission is aware of the concerns relating to the practice of traders reducing the size or quantity of consumer products while maintaining the same price and appearance of the packaging as before the reduction (‘shrinkflation’).
While EU consumer law does not limit the traders’ freedom to set retail prices or to determine the size or quantity of their products, the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive[1] (UCPD), Consumer Rights Directive[2] and sector-specific legislation, where applicable, require traders to clearly indicate the total price of a product and its main characteristics, such as size. Moreover, Article 6 of the UCPD prohibits various types of traders’ misleading commercial practices that cause or are likely to cause the average consumer to take a transactional decision that they would not have taken otherwise. Subject to a case-by-case assessment, such practices could also consist of a misleading overall presentation of the product in a way that deceives or is likely to deceive the average consumer about the product’s size.
The enforcement of EU consumer law falls under the competence of Member States. The UCPD enables national authorities and courts to assess and stop such practices when they mislead the average consumer. National authorities are aware of these practices, conduct market surveillance and take measures, where appropriate. Consumers are encouraged to report such practices to the relevant authorities in their Member State.
[1] Directive 2005/29/EC concerning unfair business-to-consumer commercial practices, OJ L 149, 11.6.2005, p 22.
[2] Directive 2011/83/EU on consumer rights, OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 64.

Earlier answer: UCPD Art. 6 may catch misleading size presentation case by case (Q1); national enforcement/market surveillance (Q3); not covered: Q2 EU action or FIC amendment.

new_question:
EU trade with Israeli settlements, illegal under international law
Recent reports following this week’s Foreign Affairs Council indicate that Member States discussed possible measures concerning EU trade relations with Israel in the light of the situation in the occupied Palestinian territories. Among the options reportedly raised was a proposal by several Member States to introduce tariffs or restrictive trade measures on products originating from illegal Israeli settlements. According to the reports, the Council did not reach a political decision at this stage but tasked the Commission with preparing possible options and scenarios for further discussion.
At the same time, trade in products from Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories contravenes international law and EU case-law. In its 2024 Advisory Opinion - mandatory for the EU and the Member States - the International Court of Justice stated that states and international organisations should refrain from actions that imply recognition of or assistance to the illegal situation arising from the occupation, including economic and trade relations. Against this backdrop, merely discussing tariffs on settlement products risks implicitly accepting the continuation of trade that is in itself illegal.
1. How can the Commission justify introducing tariffs on products for which trade is illegal under international law? Is this not a way of normalising illegal trade?
2. Does the Commission intend to fully uphold international law obligations in its trade relations with Israel?
earlier_answer:
The EU has taken good note of the advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in respect of the ‘Legal Consequences arising from the Policies and Practices of Israel in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem’[1].
The EU has a long-standing position of non-recognition of Israel’s sovereignty over the territories occupied by Israel since June 1967 and considers Israel’s settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory as illegal. EU positions are fully aligned with recent United Nations Security Council resolutions in particular 2334 and 2735[2] regarding the status of the Occupied Palestinian Territory, and EU policies are therefore overall consistent with the conclusions of the advisory opinion of the ICJ. Already since 2013, EU support in the form of grants, prizes or financial instruments must comply with the ‘Guidelines on the eligibility of Israeli entities and their activities in the territories occupied by Israel since June 1967’[3]. The EU differentiation policy implies that goods originating from Israeli settlements in territories occupied since June 1967 do not fall within the scope of the EU-Israel Association Agreement[4] and therefore cannot benefit from trade preferences under the agreement. Member States will discuss the implications of the advisory opinion on EU positions and policies further in the relevant Council preparatory bodies.
The EU has already listed nine individuals and five entities[5] under the EU Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime, for serious and systematic human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank. Any decision to list additional individuals and entities is for the Council to adopt by unanimity.

[2] https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n16/463/89/pdf/n1646389.pdf and https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/un-documents/document/s-res-2735.php
[3] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52013XC0719(03)
[4] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/resource.html?uri=cellar:411c0668-144d-44a1-a5e3-dd2342f7a5b5.0017.02/DOC_1&format=PDF
[5] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202401175 and https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202401967

new_question:
Freedom of expression and automated content - clarification of open questions on the scope of protection of fundamental rights (follow-up question to question [REF])
The Commission's answer of 18 June 2025 to question for written answer [REF][1] on protecting freedom of expression with regard to automatically generated or published content leaves fundamental questions unanswered. The blanket statement that automatically generated content ‘does not in itself enjoy any protection’ under the fundamental right to freedom of expression fails to recognise the reality of digital forms of communication and ignores the fact that such content is often based on human rules, intentions and editorial concepts. Technological change must not lead to an artificial narrowing of the protection of fundamental rights.
1. In the Commission's view, what is the legal or fundamental rights justification for excluding content that is automatically generated and published according to clearly defined human rules from the protection of freedom of expression - even if it is an expression of human intention and editorial oversight?
2. How does the Commission assess the fact that many serious journalistic offerings are also increasingly using automated systems to create and publish content (e.g. weather reports, sports reports or stock market news), and does the Commission recognise that such content can form part of the freedom of expression of the press and the freedom to express one’s opinions?
3. Why does the Commission not address the principle that, in cases of doubt - for example, where authorship is unclear - the protection of freedom of expression should be taken as the default instead of automatically deleting content or categorising it as ‘not being protected by fundamental rights’, and does the Commission plan to enshrine such a protection mechanism in existing or future legislation?
[1] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html
earlier_answer:
Freedom of expression is enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights[1] and a cherished value of the EU. It applies to all forms of expression within the scope and limits provided for in the EU Treaties, international human rights law and the national laws. Human rights are inherent to all human beings[2].
Putting people and their rights at the centre of the digital transformation are also core principles in the EU approach to digitalisation and technological advancement. Technology must support rights and democracy. It is always the individuals who may avail themselves of free expression rights and their protection. Automatically generated and published content does not in itself enjoy any protection in this respect. Artificial intelligence (AI) systems can support people’s exercise of freedom of expression and freedom of information with a variety of tools, such as search engines or translation software.
As provided for in the AI Act[3], certain AI systems intended to interact with natural persons or to generate content may pose risks of impersonation or deception. The AI Act contains rules to distinguish between AI generated content and human generated content, including rules to ensure that the use of AI systems to generate content such as deep fakes should clearly and distinguishably disclose the artificial character of the content generation. Inauthentic use or tactics involving artificially generated content, including the use of online bots, could also lead to the widespread dissemination of illegal content online and contribute to disinformation campaigns. The Digital Services Act provides obligations for providers of very large online platforms and very large online search engines to assess and mitigate systemic risks stemming from their services, including negative effects on freedom of expression[4]. They shall act in a diligent, objective and proportionate manner in applying content moderation restrictions, with due regard to freedom of expression.
[1] Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, OJ C 326, 26.10.2012, p. 391-407.
[2] United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 1948, https://www.un.org/en/about-us/universal-declaration-of-human-rights.
[3] Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence, OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj.
[4] Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market for Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act), OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, p. 1-102.

new_question:

A study recently published by the journal Current Biology revealed serious irregularities in the trade of caviar and sturgeon in the Lower Danube countries. An analysis of approximately 150 samples revealed that 21 % were illegal catches, 30 % violated CITES rules and 32 % had labels with false information on the sturgeon species or the country where they were caught. The samples of sturgeon and caviar meat were purchased in restaurants, fish markets and bars. Although strict labelling rules were introduced in 2000 to protect those species from illegal trade, the practices uncovered by this analysis warn of the need to improve the existing controls. These illegal activities, which are not sustainable, are having an impact on the critical situation of this species in the Danube and urgent action is needed.
1. Does the Commission have any information to back up the Current Biology report?
2. What influence are these practices having on the critical situation of this species in the Danube?
3. Does the Commission intend to take any specific steps to address this situation?
earlier_answer:
The Commission is strongly committed to sturgeon conservation. The Habitats Directive[1] lists all six sturgeon species that have historically occurred in the Lower Danube Basin. Therefore, their conservation is a legal obligation for the EU Member States.
In May 2019, the EU nature directives sub-expert group (NADEG) recommended the Pan-European Action Plan for Sturgeons[2] for implementation. This Action Plan was adopted in 2018 under the Bern Convention[3], to which the EU and the Member States are parties, and lists close to 70 actions to restore sturgeon populations in the Pan-European region. The Commission closely follows its implementation.
EU funds supported several projects aimed at conserving Europe’s sturgeon species. The MEASURES project[4] aimed to create ecological corridors along the Danube and its main tributaries. Both sturgeons and other migratory fish species benefit from these actions. The EU programme for the environment and climate action (LIFE) for Danube Sturgeons project[5] - that supported the World Wildlife Fund study mentioned in the question - aimed to find solutions to stop the threat that illegal fishing and trade pose to sturgeons in the Lower Danube Basin and north-western Black Sea region. The authors analysed Danish reporting data on Pfizer/BioNTech (BNT162b2) and found that the number of suspected cases of adverse events varied considerably between batches. They described clusters of batches with different rates of reporting and identified these as a ‘batch-dependent safety signal’. The authors called for further study on the matter.
- Manniche et al. (2024), ‘Reports of Batch-Dependent Suspected Adverse Events of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 Vaccine: Comparison of Results from Denmark and Sweden’, Journal: Medicines[2]. This study compared suspected cases in Denmark and Sweden. The authors reported that similar patterns of variation between batches had been observed in both countries. They stressed that the results were preliminary and hypothesis-generating.

2. Does the Commission know what variation has been observed between batches of mRNA vaccines in quality controls, and is there also variation between EU Member States?
3. Has the Commission launched investigations into published observations regarding variations in adverse reaction reports between batches?

earlier_answer:
The Commission is in contact with Member States and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) to ensure the continuous quality, safety and efficacy of medicines, including COVID-19 vaccines.
EMA continuously monitors safety signals and investigates whether there is a causal link between specific batches and reported adverse events. EMA has no evidence so far suggesting that some batches of Comirnaty caused more (or more serious) side effects than other batches[1]. The quality of every batch is checked by Official Medicines Control Laboratories in Member States and only those complying with the approved quality specifications can be released in the EU.
Regulators request and collect batch numbers for vaccines to allow them to establish patterns and determine whether suspected side effects are linked to a specific batch. The Paul-Ehrlich-Institut (PEI) reports suspected side effects with Comirnaty, but it does not confirm these as side effects, nor does it link them to specific batches. The conditional marketing authorisation was converted into a standard marketing authorisation on 10 October 2022. After authorisation in 2020, EMA has been continuously monitoring suspected side effects and evaluating any new information that emerges[2]. This evaluation is conducted by EMA's expert committees, and action is taken, if necessary.
Comirnaty continues to fulfil the necessary requirements for authorisation in the EU.

1. The Union Customs Code provides that customs authorities may retain goods when necessary to carry out checks to ensure compliance with EU law. Such checks must be carried out within a reasonable period and, where appropriate, lead to a formal decision subject to appeal. The present reply is based on the assumption that the case concerns the application of customs legislation.
The primary responsibility for the implementation of EU restrictive measures rests with the competent authorities of Member States. The Commission provides on its website the contact details of all such authorities[2], and has set up, at EU level, dedicated contact points to answer questions on these measures from economic operators[3].

new_question:
EU-prescribed diesel engine additive does not work in freezing conditions
Finland has recently experienced severe frosts throughout the country. The lowest temperature recorded so far this year has been -42.8°C, in Lapland. It has become apparent that EU legislation does not take enough account of the different weather conditions in the Member States. Furthermore, sufficient requirements are not in place obliging vehicle manufacturers to take into account the reliability of emission reduction systems in cold conditions such as those commonly experienced in Finland.
Current emission reduction equipment for diesel cars cannot withstand Finnish winter temperatures, and up to 80 % of transport companies have experienced problems owing to the AdBlue urea solution freezing. In practice, AdBlue fluid is required by the EU to reduce nitrogen oxide emissions, but it freezes at around -11°C.
The problem is widespread, as the freezing of the AdBlue urea solution increases the risk of equipment failure, affecting not only cars but machinery as well, and resulting in significant additional costs for sectors such as transport, forestry, agriculture, mining, public transport and tourism. The vulnerability of the systems to normal freezing conditions is also having a negative impact on Finland’s security of supply.
1. Is the Commission aware that the AdBlue urea solution, which is effectively required under by EU regulations, does not work in normal winter conditions in Finland, causing unnecessary additional costs and having an adverse impact on Finland’s security of supply?
2. Will the Commission permit, as a matter of urgency, alternative, more frost-resistant additives to reduce nitrogen oxide emissions from diesel cars?
3. Does the Commission intend to take better account of northern conditions, and of the specific characteristics of the north, in EU regulation in the future?
earlier_answer:
The Euro 6 regulatory framework[1] does not stipulate the use of a urea solution (AdBlue or others) to control emissions, but it does set requirements for emission control systems that use a reagent. For Euro 6 vehicles using a reagent to control emissions, manufacturers must ensure that the emission control system retains its emission control function during all ambient conditions, especially at low ambient temperatures. This includes taking measures to prevent the complete freezing of the reagent during parking times of up to seven days at minus 15 °C with the reagent tank fifty per cent full. If the reagent has frozen, the manufacturer must ensure that the reagent is available for use within 20 minutes of the vehicle starting at minus 15 °C. Euro 6 requirements for vehicles that use a reagent for the exhaust after-treatment system mirror those of United Nations Regulation No 154[2].
Commercial AdBlue is already engineered to have the lowest possible freezing point. Nonetheless, existing EU emission regulations would allow for improved reagents with lower freezing points to be placed on the market. No standardisation work on reagents is currently foreseen by the Commission.
The Commission is not aware of low-temperature conditions leading to the need to repair after-treatment systems in Euro 6 vehicles and would be interested in more information on the Finnish study with regard to this topic.
[1] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2007/715/oj; https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2009/595/oj
[2] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:42021X2039 (see Appendix 6).
notes: Asks: Q1 aware AdBlue fails in Finnish winter, costs/supply security; Q2 allow frost-resistant alternative additives; Q3 consider northern conditions in future rules. Earlier answer: Euro 6 does not mandate urea, anti-freeze requirements at -15 C, rules already allow improved lower-freezing reagents (Q2), not aware of repair needs (Q1); not covered: Q3, non-road machinery, security of supply.
