1. Can the Commission state the factors it considered and procedure it followed when formulating the opinion it was asked to give on the compatibility of the right of pre-emption granted in the tender with EU principles?
2. To what extent might this opinion impact the tender for the concession, and what are the possible repercussions in the event of a verdict of incompatibility with EU rules?
3. Given the strategic importance of the A22 and the need to ensure that the goals of sustainable mobility, decarbonisation and the protection of public health are pursued, is there any scope for an in-house award of the concession to a fully public company?
earlier_answer:
A concession such as the A22 motorway concession may be awarded without a call for tenders if the in-house requirements under Article 17 of the Concessions Directive are fulfilled[1].
If not all the in-house requirements, including the absence of private capital in the concessionaire company, were fulfilled, the concession would have to be awarded via a call for tenders ensuring fair competition.
However, any eventual participation of the incumbent concessionaire in the tendering procedure should be accompanied by the adoption of the appropriate mitigation measures to ensure that competition is not distorted.
The Commission supports the transition towards zero emission mobility and a modal shift towards sustainable mobility solutions, as shown by recent initiatives included in the second Mobility Package[2], such as the proposal for a new trans-European transport network (TEN-T) Regulation[3], the new Urban Mobility Framework and the Rail Action Plan to boost long-distance and cross-border passenger transport. While it is the prerogative of Member States to design and implement transport policies for the different modes of transport, the Commission will continue to ensure conformity of Member States’ actions with Union law and support initiatives consistent with the above broad EU policy objectives.
[1] Directive 2014/23/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 February 2014 on the award of concession contracts (OJ L 094 28.3.2014, p. 1).
[2] https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-modes/road/mobility-package-questions-and-answers_en
[3] https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/qanda_21_6725
notes: Asks: Q1 factors and procedure behind the Commission's opinion on the A22 tender's pre-emption right; Q2 the opinion's potential impact and consequences of incompatibility; Q3 scope for an in-house award to a fully public company. Earlier answer: an in-house award is possible if all Article 17 Concessions Directive requirements are met, including absence of private capital; otherwise a competitive tender is required, with measures to prevent distortion if the incumbent participates; it also discusses sustainable mobility; not covered: the pre-emption opinion, its basis or consequences.

new_question:
Inclusion of surrogacy in the new EU strategy to combat trafficking in human beings
During the joint hearing of 3 June 2026 of Parliament’s Committees on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs and on Women’s Rights and Gender Equality concerning the forthcoming strategy to combat trafficking in human beings, the Commission’s EU Anti-Trafficking Coordinator, Diane Schmitt, stated that surrogacy would not be included in the strategy.
This statement is surprising, given that Directive (EU) 2024/1712[1], which amended Directive 2011/36/EU on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings, expressly included surrogacy among the forms of exploitation that Member States must classify as trafficking in human beings. Furthermore, in its news article of 12 July 2024 on the entry into force of the new anti-trafficking rules[2], the Commission itself highlighted that the exploitation of surrogacy is one of the new forms of exploitation covered by the legislative revision.
Can the Commission clarify:
1. whether it considers surrogacy to constitute a form of trafficking in human beings within the meaning of Directive (EU) 2024/1712?
2. whether it intends to explicitly include measures to combat surrogacy in the forthcoming EU strategy to combat trafficking in human beings?
3. what concrete initiatives it intends to adopt to tackle transnational criminal networks involved in cross-border surrogacy arrangements and the sale of children?
[1] Directive (EU) 2024/1712 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 amending Directive 2011/36/EU on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting its victims (OJ L, 2024/1712, 24.6.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1712/oj).
[2] European Commission ‘Stronger EU rules to fight trafficking in human beings enter into force’, news article, 12 July 2024, https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/news/stronger-eu-rules-fight-trafficking-human-beings-enter-force-2024-07-12_en.
earlier_answer:
The Commission is committed to upholding children’s and women’s rights within the framework of its competences.
The exploitation of surrogacy, among others, is included as a form of exploitation in the Anti-Trafficking Directive, modified by Directive (EU) 2024/1712 of 13 June 2024[1]. It targets those who coerce or deceive women into acting as surrogate mothers, without prejudice to the national rules on surrogacy, including criminal and family law.
Substantive family law, such as rules on the definition of family and rules on surrogacy, falls exclusively within the competence of the Member States. Each Member State therefore decides its policy and legal position as regards surrogacy. Some Member States allow and regulate surrogacy, some Member States prohibit it, and other Member States do not have a specific legal framework.
The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union applies to the EU institutions in all their actions. However, it does not extend the competences conferred on the EU by the Treaties[2].
[1] https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1712/oj/eng.
[2] Article 51 of the Charter: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A12016P%2FTXT.
notes: Asks: Q1 whether surrogacy constitutes trafficking under Directive 2024/1712; Q2 whether measures against surrogacy will be included in the forthcoming strategy; Q3 initiatives against cross-border surrogacy networks and child sale. Earlier answer: exploitation of surrogacy is included as a form of exploitation in the amended directive, targeting coercion or deception of surrogate mothers; substantive surrogacy law is a Member State competence; not covered: the forthcoming strategy or the requested initiatives.

new_question:
‘Stop Destroying Videogames’ European Citizens’ Initiative
The European Citizens’ Initiative ‘Stop Destroying Videogames’ has collected over 1.2 million signatures from EU citizens. The breadth of support shows that this issue is important to players, i.e. European consumers.
Videogames are not just a form of entertainment nowadays; they play an important role in education, socialisation, culture and sport. The largest AAA productions cost up to EUR 60-70 on the day of their release.
However, many games are designed in such a way that they cease to function after technical support provided by the producer ends, regardless of whether or not the consumer has purchased the game.
This raises serious legal and ethical questions: can consumers be prevented from using a purchased product solely because the producer considered it unprofitable to maintain this product, and should rules not be adopted stating that it is consumers who have the right to decide when to stop using a product they have purchased, rather than the person who produced the product?
These practices also raise questions in the context of the European circular economy policy, which aims to combat waste and planned obsolescence.
In light of the above:
1. Is the Commission considering drawing up realistic and enforceable regulations in relation to this issue?
2. Is the Commission also considering addressing price differences on the European gaming market, including higher prices in countries such as Poland?
earlier_answer:
The Commission is aware of the European citizens’ initiative Stop killing Videogames.
EU consumer protection legislation does not set specific duration for the supply of digital content/service but requires traders to supply it in accordance with the contract and consumer’s reasonable expectations.
Under Directive 2019/770/EU[1] the discontinuation of the digital content/service by the trader sooner than what was contractually agreed or what the consumer may reasonably expect would constitute lack of conformity with the contract. The trader can deviate from the objective requirements for conformity if it has specifically informed the consumer and the latter had expressly and separately accepted such deviation at the time of the conclusion of the contract. In the case of a lack of conformity, the consumer can terminate the contract causing the supplier’s obligation to refund part of the price paid.
Modern video game distribution models typically require users to agree to the terms and conditions governing their licensed use. Although these terms may differ between vendors, the licenses acquired are not perpetual. Such licensing conditions are part of the contract between the provider and consumer.
[1] Directive (EU) 2019/770 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 May 2019 on certain aspects concerning contracts for the supply of digital content and digital services, OJ L 136, 22.5.2019, p. 1-27.
notes: Asks: Q1 whether the Commission is considering enforceable rules concerning games ceasing to work after producer support ends; Q2 whether it is considering EU gaming price differences, including higher prices in Poland. Earlier answer: it is aware of the initiative; Directive 2019/770 addresses contractual conformity and reasonable expectations when digital services are discontinued, with possible remedies; it describes typical licensed-use terms as not perpetual; not covered: plans for new rules or price differences.

new_question:
Measures to prevent and limit the impact of extreme climate events
Cyclone Boris has had a devastating effect on several countries in central and eastern Europe, and has unfortunately led to loss of life. We express our sincere condolences to all the bereaved families in Romania, Poland and Austria. We also express our solidarity with those affected in Czechia, Slovakia and the Republic of Moldova.
As the European Parliament’s lead negotiator on the EU budget, I support an increase in the budget for financial instruments to address emergencies and disasters both in terms of the Civil Protection Mechanism and of compensation and investment in their prevention.
Against the backdrop of these extreme phenomena and natural disasters, which are increasing in number and intensity, what proposals and financing is the Commission advocating to prevent and limit the impact of climate events on the public?
earlier_answer:
1. The inter-institutional agreement accompanying the 2021-2027 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) includes a commitment to spend at least 30% of all resources available under the 2021-2027 MFF and NextGenerationEU to address climate objectives, including adaptation. The Common Provisions Regulation[1] that governs the European Regional Development Fund, the European Social Fund Plus, the Cohesion Fund, the Just Transition Fund and the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund, further requires climate proofing to be an integral part of programming and implementation of these funds. Within that framework, it is paramount to consider the need to create resilience through all major decisions.
In the area of civil protection, the Commission adopted a Recommendation and Communication[2] setting out Union disaster resilience goals for 2027-2030, which highlight the need of considering the impact of climate change on disaster risks. Under the Union Civil Protection Mechanism, funds are available for cross-border prevention and preparedness projects to help Member and Participating States to implement the disaster resilience goals and thereby try to adapt to climate change.
2. The Commission proposed in June 2023, in the context of the MFF mid-term revision 2023, a EUR 2.5 billion increase of the Solidarity and Emergency Aid Reserve to reinforce the EU’s capacity to address crises and emergency situations.
3. The MFF proposal for the post-2027 period is due by 30 June 2025. It is too early for the Commission to indicate the funding for specific sectors and areas of intervention.
[1] Regulation (EU) 2021/1060 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2021 laying down common provisions on the European Regional Development Fund, the European Social Fund Plus, the Cohesion Fund, the Just Transition Fund and the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund and financial rules for those and for the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund, the Internal Security Fund and the Instrument for Financial Support for Border Management and Visa Policy, OJ L 231, 30.6.2021, p. 159-706.

new_question:
Natural disasters caused by climate change
Recently a number of countries have been hit by natural disasters with extreme weather conditions causing deadly forest fires and flooding, leading to many areas being evacuated and leaving thousands of people displaced. Greece was especially hard-hit by wildfires, notably in Rhodes, Attica, Evros and Thessaly. In light of these disasters, our thoughts are constantly with the inhabitants of the affected areas, with the women and men working for the fire service, the security forces and the volunteers who fought to keep people safe.
In view of this:
1. Will the Commission take any additional prevention measures to protect nature and human safety and address the effects of climate change, thereby supporting areas that have taken a hit economically?
2. Will it review the Civil Protection Mechanism, which should be adapted to address the ever-growing consequences of climate change and monitor the funding that will be given to affected countries?
3. Will it increase funding in the budget to support Member States and review the Solidarity Fund so that more help is given to countries affected by natural disasters caused by climate change?
earlier_answer:
1. In the proposal for the Nature Restoration Regulation[1], for which a provisional agreement has been reached with the co-legislators, Member States are required to put in place measures to improve areas of habitat types listed in Annex I which are not in good condition. This includes forest habitats. It also proposed to put in place restoration measures necessary to enhance biodiversity in the wider forest ecosystems. The reforestation guidelines referred at by the Honourable Member are voluntary.
2. The Commission expects continued and strong warming to drive a further increase of wildfire risks in Europe, including in areas where they were not a major challenge so far. The EU is already investing in climate mitigation, climate adaptation, and disaster preparedness and response to prevent the most destructive and costly climate scenarios. Avoiding losses entirely may not be possible, but investing in long-term prevention will be cheaper than paying the damages and losses caused by wildfires, as with other climate driven hazards. It is therefore of utmost importance that investing in wildfire prevention at EU, national, regional and local levels is a priority, with the objective of creating less fire-prone and more fire-resilient landscapes that can recover quickly.
3. Member States’ Rural Development Programmes 2014-2022[2] and the Common Agricultural Policy Strategic Plans 2023-2027[3] are available to support the restoration of both agricultural and forest ecosystems following natural disasters, adverse climatic or catastrophic events, and investments in appropriate preventive action. The EU Solidarity Fund[4] may cover part of the costs for emergency and recovery operations incurred by public authorities. Moreover, the Commission proposed[5] in June 2023 a EUR 2.5 billion increase of the Solidarity and Emergency Aid Reserve[6] for the remaining four years of the 2021-27 Multiannual Financial Framework[7] to reinforce EU’s capacity to address crises and emergency situations.
[1] https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/nature-and-biodiversity/nature-restoration-law_en
[2] https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy/rural-development/country_en
[3] https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy/cap-overview/cap-2023-27_en
[4] https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/funding/solidarity-fund_en
[5] In June 2023 in the context of the Multiannual Financial Framework mid-term revision 2023.
[6] https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/eu-budget/long-term-eu-budget/2021-2027/spending/flexibility-and-special-instruments_en#solidarity-and-emergency-aid-reserve-sear
[7] https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/eu-budget/long-term-eu-budget/2021-2027_en
notes: Asks: Q1 extra prevention measures/support for hit areas; Q2 review of UCPM and monitoring of funding; Q3 more budget and Solidarity Fund review. Earlier answer: Nature Restoration Regulation forest measures (Q1), wildfire prevention priority (Q1), RDP/CAP restoration support, EUSF, EUR 2.5bn SEAR increase proposal (Q3); not covered: Q2 UCPM review, Solidarity Fund review, Greece specifically.

new_question:
Accountability of Airbus in the Privatisation of TAP
The Inspectorate-General of Finance of the Portuguese Republic has carried out an audit that points to the participation of Airbus - a European multinational - in an illegal and criminal scheme for financing TAP’s privatisation in 2015.
The same conclusion had already been reached by a Portuguese Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry, whose work was completed a year ago. At that time, the Assembly of the Republic asked the Government to request that the European Union investigate that participation and establish the necessary accountabilities for the difficulties that said participation created for the Portuguese Republic.
In the meantime, the Portuguese Prime Minister has informed the Assembly of the Republic that the Government has not taken ‘any steps’ to implement that resolution of the Assembly of the Republic. This was a regrettable choice, but one that only serves to hold accountable those to made it (the last two Portuguese governments).
But the question was already referred directly to the European Commission (questions [REF][1] and [REF][2]), so we are asking again:
1. Has the European Commission already carried out an assessment of the role played by Airbus in the privatisation process of TAP, in 2015, and its accountability for the damage caused to the Portuguese Republic by that privatisation?

[2] https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/[REF]_EN.html

The Commission is not in a position to comment on the circumstances referred in the Honourable Member’s question, which, to the Commission’s knowledge, are the subject matter of an ongoing investigation at the national level.

new_question:
Bluetongue epidemic - challenges facing sheep farmers in Portugal
Sheep farming in Portugal has been severely hit by the bluetongue virus epidemic, which, according to the National Confederation of Agricultural Cooperatives and Agricultural Credit of Portugal, ‘has wiped out thousands of sheep across the country and could spread to bovine animals’.
According to the National Confederation of Agriculture (CNA), ‘data from the system on the collection of the cadavers of animals that die on farms (SIRCA) show that the disease is out of control and containment measures are needed right away’.
There are also concerns that SIRCA could collapse.
Both bodies are calling for an immediate and free vaccination campaign and for extraordinary support to cover animal losses, as well as treatment and prevention costs, given that the costs arising from this situation are beyond the means of the vast majority of farms.
As farmers face an unanticipated decline in livestock numbers, the CNA is also warning about the risk of them being penalised by the blanket application of rules under the common agricultural policy (CAP).
In view of the above:
1. Is the Commission aware of a request from the Portuguese Government for the deployment of resources to this end?
2. Will it allow measures adapting the CAP rules to avoid penalising farmers affected by a decline in livestock numbers?
earlier_answer:
The Commission is aware of difficulties caused by bluetongue which have been discussed at the Agriculture and Fisheries Council on 23 September 2024.
Member States may implement eradication programmes[1]. They must maintain a publicly available up-to-date list of disease-free areas. Movements of animals from affected zones must comply with risk mitigation measures[2] and certification. Member States have a long experience in combating bluetongue and coordinating among themselves.
The EU can provide financial support under the Common Market Organisation upon evidence that the market is affected by trade restrictions, resulting from the application of veterinary measures for combating the spread of the disease.
Strategic Plans may provide support to prevent and mitigate the economic impacts of animal diseases. Support can be provided for risk management, improving on-farm biosecurity and investments to restore agricultural potential that Member States are encouraged to use. An additional support possibility has been put forward by the Commission on 21 October 2024, proposing to introduce adaptations to the European agricultural fund for rural development (EAFRD) 2014-2022 programmes to allow Member States to provide emergency support of up to EUR 42 000 to farmers affected by natural disasters (including animal diseases) or to reinforce measures to restore production potential.
Aid for the prevention, control and eradication of animal diseases and to compensate for the damage caused by them may be granted under certain conditions by Member States, without prior notification, under the Agricultural Block Exemption Regulation[3] or, with prior notification, under the Agricultural State aid Guidelines[4]. Limited support can also be granted in application of the Agricultural de minimis Regulation[5].
[1] Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/689 of 17 December 2019 supplementing Regulation (EU) 2016/429 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards rules for surveillance, eradication programmes, and disease-free status for certain listed and emerging diseases: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2020/689/oj
[2] For example, with vaccination.
[3] Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/2472 of 14 December 2022 declaring certain categories of aid in the agricultural and forestry sectors and in rural areas compatible with the internal market in application of Articles 107 and 108 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European (OJ L 327, 21.12.2022, p. 1).
[4] Guidelines for State aid in the agricultural and forestry sectors and in rural areas (OJ C 485, 21.12.2022, p. 1-90).
[5] Commission Regulation (EU) No 1408/2013 of 18 December 2013 on the application of Articles 107 and 108 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union to de minimis aid in the agriculture sector (OJ L 352, 24.12.2013, p. 9).

Earlier answer: aware of bluetongue (Sept 2024 Council), eradication programmes, CMO support, Strategic Plan risk mgmt, EAFRD emergency support up to EUR 42k, State aid options; not covered: Q1 Portuguese request, Q2 CAP penalty adaptation.

new_question:
The death of Mahmoud Bakhum in Seville as he was pursued by police
The recent death of Mahmoud Bakhum, a street vendor in Seville who, panicked by a police chase, fell into the River Guadalquivir, shows just how serious reports of racial bias in police action are.
A number of reports drawn up by Spain’s ombudsman and human rights organisations document continuing practices, such as racial profiling, which perpetuate discrimination and breach fundamental rights.
What is more, it is apparent that there are barriers to properly reporting such practices and resistance within institutions to acknowledging the problem.
Is the Commission considering proposing an EU mechanism to monitor, collect data and act in cases of institutional racism in security forces?
earlier_answer:
Member States are responsible for maintaining law and order and safeguarding internal security, and any action by national authorities, including national police officers, remains the responsibility of the Member State concerned, Greece in this instance. As set out in its reply to written questions [REF], [REF] and [REF], and as recalled during the European Parliament plenary session debate of 20 October 2020 on police brutality[1], the Commission strongly condemns the disproportionate use of force or violence, and any form of discrimination by police forces. Member States should promote and respect their law enforcement rules of conduct in full respect of their European and international human rights obligations. National authorities must investigate individual cases of reported police brutality and ensure that justice is served. Member States must also ensure the correct implementation and application in practice of Directive 2013/48/EU on the right of access to a lawyer and Directive (EU) 2016/800 on procedural safeguards for children who are suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings. The Commission is closely monitoring the implementation of these directives.

new_question:
Police infiltration in social movements in Spain, and its impact on fundamental rights
In Spain, there have recently been cases of officers in the National Police Force having infiltrated people’s lives and social movements using false identities. These actions violate the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, which prohibits inhuman and degrading treatment and protects the rights to, and freedoms of, expression, association and assembly. In addition, under Spanish law, these practices could constitute offences both against the inviolability of the home, and of the disclosure of secrets. The provisions of a Franco-era law on official secrets mean we cannot determine how many police officers have infiltrated social movements. That law is one that the European Commission has already asked Spain to review, since it is at odds with the rule of law.
1. Does the Commission consider that police infiltration in social movements in Spain violates the above fundamental rights and, therefore, the rule of law?
2. Does the Commission consider these practices to endanger the protection of human rights, and what measures does it intend to adopt to ensure that Spain respects and protects these rights in the context of police actions?
3. What is the Commission’s assessment of the continued application of the Spanish Law on Official Secrets?
earlier_answer:
The Commission has no specific information on the situation referred to by the Honourable Member.
As set out in its reply to written question [REF], internal security matters, including actions by national authorities for the purpose of maintaining law and order and safeguarding internal security, remain the responsibility of the Member State concerned. Consequently, policing matters, such as the one referred to by the Honourable Member, fall within the remit of the Spanish authorities. Specific matters of fundamental rights and policing also do not fall within the scope of the Rule of Law report.
The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union applies to Member States when they are implementing EU law[1]. Outside those situations, it is for Member States, including their judicial authorities, to ensure that fundamental rights are effectively respected and protected in accordance with their national legislation and international human rights obligations.
[1] Article 51(1) EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.
notes: Asks: Q1 whether police infiltration of Spanish social movements breaches fundamental rights and the rule of law; Q2 whether it endangers human rights and what measures the Commission intends to take; Q3 its assessment of the continued application of Spain's Official Secrets Law. Earlier answer: it has no specific information on the situation; policing is Spain's responsibility and specific fundamental-rights and policing matters are outside the Rule of Law report's scope; the Charter applies to Member States when implementing EU law, and otherwise national authorities must protect rights; not covered: an assessment of the specific practices or intended measures, or an assessment of the Official Secrets Law.

new_question:
mRNA COVID-19 vaccines in Europe: transparency in batch testing and adverse reaction reports
Several reports suggest considerable variation in adverse reactions to individual batches of mRNA vaccines. Here are two examples:
Schmeling, Manniche and Hansen (2023), ‘Batch-dependent safety of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine’, Journal: European Journal of Clinical Investigation[1]. The authors analysed Danish reporting data on Pfizer/BioNTech (BNT162b2) and found that the number of suspected cases of adverse events varied considerably between batches. They described clusters of batches with different rates of reporting and identified these as a ‘batch-dependent safety signal’. The authors called for further study on the matter.
- Manniche et al. (2024), ‘Reports of Batch-Dependent Suspected Adverse Events of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 Vaccine: Comparison of Results from Denmark and Sweden’, Journal: Medicines[2]. This study compared suspected cases in Denmark and Sweden. The authors reported that similar patterns of variation between batches had been observed in both countries. They stressed that the results were preliminary and hypothesis-generating.
1. Does the Commission know what independent assessments have been carried out on individual batches of mRNA vaccines, and what conclusion was drawn?
2. Does the Commission know what variation has been observed between batches of mRNA vaccines in quality controls, and is there also variation between EU Member States?
3. Has the Commission launched investigations into published observations regarding variations in adverse reaction reports between batches?
[1] https://research.regionh.dk/en/publications/batch-dependent-safety-of-the-bnt162b2-mrna-covid-19-vaccine/.
[2] https://research.regionh.dk/en/publications/reports-of-batch-dependent-suspected-adverse-events-of-the-bnt162/.
earlier_answer:
As for any other medicinal products authorised in the EU, once a COVID-19 vaccine has received approval, each vaccine batch can only be released following quality control testing to confirm that the product is in line with the specifications that were approved as part of the respective marketing authorisation. This control is carried out by the manufacturer. However, for most centrally authorised vaccines, the EU legislation requires that a Member State Official Medicines Control Laboratory performs an additional independent control for each batch before it is put on the EU market. This independent control is referred to as Official Control Authority Batch Release testing and includes testing of agreed quality parameters and a compliance check of the manufacturer’s own test results.
The Danish study looked at a potential link between serious adverse events cases and vaccine batch labels reported to the Danish Medicines Agency. As highlighted by the authors themselves, there are several limitations when carrying out a study on data from passive surveillance such as this one.
Pharmacovigilance systems are in place to monitor the suspected adverse reactions (AR), which include medical literature monitoring and a product quality issue detection algorithm to detect safety issues potentially related to quality.
As regards literature monitoring, if various sources of information point to a potential issue more in-depth review is initiated. This was not the case for the mentioned Danish study. In addition to the limitations mentioned in the study, analyses performed by the European Medicines Agency on the batches reported in suspected AR cases did not reveal an increased risk of side effects for specific batches.
notes: Asks: Q1 what independent assessments of individual mRNA vaccine batches were carried out and their conclusions; Q2 observed quality-control variation between batches and Member States; Q3 investigations into published observations of variation in adverse-reaction reports between batches. Earlier answer: manufacturers test batches and, for most centrally authorised vaccines, an official laboratory independently checks each batch before release; the Danish study had limitations and did not trigger a deeper literature review; EMA analyses found no increased side-effect risk for specific batches; not covered: observed quality-control variation across batches or Member States, or the 2024 Denmark–Sweden study.

new_question:
Ivermectin was and continues to be permitted for use in the treatment of COVID-19
The Austrian Supreme Administrative Court ruled in a final judgment that ivermectin was and continues to be permitted to be prescribed for the treatment of COVID-19[1].
Doctors are obliged to provide conscientious care to patients. This may even go beyond ‘conventional medical’ knowledge if the patient’s well-being so warrants it. What matters is whether a medicine is necessary. There is extensive scientific literature on ivermectin, as well as clinical experience from doctors, which proves precisely this[2]. Ivermectin has been successfully and safely used against COVID-19 throughout the world, including in several EU Member States. EMA and WHO recommendations to use ivermectin only in clinical trials are not legally binding. Guidelines cannot replace the treating physician’s expertise and freedom to choose a course of treatment.
1. Why was ivermectin, which has been on the WHO list of essential medicines for decades, not recommended by the Commission and the EMA for the treatment of COVID-19?
2. Why was the use of ivermectin even hindered by the Commission and the EMA using all means available?
3. What conclusions does the Commission draw from the fact that, according to scientific literature, around half of the COVID-19 deaths in the EU could have been prevented if the patients had received ivermectin?
[1] https://www.ris.bka.gv.at/Dokument.wxe?SkipToDocumentPage=True&Abfrage=Vwgh&Dokumentnummer=JWT_2025090078_20260223L00.
[2] https://c19early.org/imeta.html.
earlier_answer:
Ivermectin medicines are not authorised for use in COVID-19 in the EU and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) has not received any application for such use either. In March 2021, EMA reviewed the latest publications and concluded that the use of ivermectin for prevention or treatment of COVID-19 cannot currently be recommended outside controlled clinical trials due to the risk of toxicity at higher than approved doses (which would be required to achieve a sufficiently high level to be effective against severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-Cov-2))[1]. This advice is also in line with the World Health Organization and other major regulators recommendations.
Vaccination is the main tool for primary prevention of transmissible disease and one of the most effective public health interventions available against serious, preventable, and sometimes deadly, contagious diseases. Thanks to widespread vaccination, smallpox has been eradicated, Europe made polio-free, and many other diseases almost eliminated. This has been the Commission’s paradigm in the past and for the COVID-19 pandemic.
Vaccination against COVID-19 offers the best preventive protection against infection, severe disease, long-term consequences of illness and loss of life. In parallel, the Commission is ensuring that COVID-19 therapeutics[2] are available to treat those who are infected.
Regarding the second question, EMA monitors the safety of COVID-19 vaccines[3] authorised in the EU extremely carefully and publishes the available information in a transparent way[4]. For example, in April, EMA published information including statistics on very rare cases of unusual blood clots with low blood platelets after vaccination with Vaxzevria[5].

[2] https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/IP_21_5366
[3] https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/human-regulatory/overview/public-health-threats/coronavirus-disease-covid-19/treatments-vaccines/vaccines-covid-19/safety-covid-19-vaccines

Earlier answer: not authorised for COVID, no application; EMA March 2021 advises against use outside trials (toxicity), aligned with WHO (Q1); vaccination as main tool; not covered: Q2 hindrance, Q3.

new_question:
Tasers cause the death of a person at the hands the police in Torremolinos
On Sunday 7 December 2025, Haitam died of a heart attack after being subdued by eight national police officers in Torremolinos. He was hit by Tasers - which can deliver up to 1 200 volts - at least three times. Images of the scene show police officers immobilising him and threating to taser him again, while cries of pain can be heard. International bodies, including the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture, warn that electroshock weapons can cause death if used repeatedly or for prolonged immobilisation.
In the past year, at least four other racialised people have died in police action, revealing a pattern of racist police violence. This constitutes a breach by Spain of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and of the obligation to ensure proportional and accountable policing, as the Commission highlights in its rule of law reports.
In light of the above:
1. Does the Commission intend to ask the Spanish Government to provide explanations for those deaths?
2. Does it plan to specifically examine the use of Tasers by Member States’ police forces?
3. Does it intend to promote, at EU level, limitations on, or the ban of, Tasers, as well as greater obligations to monitor the use of force?
earlier_answer:
The Commission condemns any form of violence. Violence runs counter to the common values upon which the EU is built.
As the Commission set out in its reply to written questions [REF], [REF], [REF], [REF], [REF] and [REF], any use of force by law enforcement authorities should always be exercised in a proportionate manner. Inhumane or degrading treatment of any individual is unacceptable.
Maintenance of law and order is primarily a competence of the Member States. They must promote and ensure respect of fundamental rights as provided for in their constitutional order and under their international law commitments.
In the case referred to by the Honourable Member, it is therefore for the Spanish authorities to conduct independent and accountable investigations leading to the determination of all relevant facts, in accordance with national legislation and international human rights obligations.
notes: Asks: Q1 ask Spain to explain Torremolinos and other police deaths; Q2 examine Taser use by MS police; Q3 EU limits/ban on Tasers, use-of-force monitoring. Earlier answer: condemns violence, force must be proportionate, policing is MS competence, Spanish authorities must investigate (Spanish case, touches Q1); not covered: Q2, Q3 Tasers and EU use-of-force rules.
